title: You are hired for judgement, not for tools
description: Why the job is deciding what to do, not knowing which vendor to recommend — and how those two things get confused in the first meeting.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a judgement call from a tool recommendation
Recognise when a client's stated request is actually a request for a tool, not a diagnosis

contentSections.title: What the client is actually asking for

contentSections.body:
First call with a new client, a six-location dental group called Larkspur Dental. The practice owner opens with: "We looked at three AI tools for insurance verification. Can you just tell us which one to buy?"

That is a completely reasonable question to ask a friend. It is the wrong question to pay a consultant for, and if you answer it as asked, you'll spend the engagement picking a vendor for a process nobody has actually looked at yet.

A client can compare vendor demos themselves — most vendors are happy to run one. What they can't do themselves, or they wouldn't have called you, is know **whether their insurance-verification problem is a tool problem at all.**

That's the judgement call: is the bottleneck the manual data entry (a tool problem), the fact that three different front-desk staff enter insurer names three different ways (a data-standards problem no tool fixes), or the fact that one specific insurer's phone queue averages 40 minutes (a problem no software touches)? A vendor demo answers none of these questions, because a vendor demo is designed to make their product look good against whatever you brought to it.

You are being paid to know which question to ask before anyone opens a laptop.

contentSections.scenario: Larkspur's owner sends you last month's three vendor demo recordings and asks for your "expert opinion on which one to buy." You watch all three. Two responses are on the table for your reply.
contentSections.question: Which response is the judgement call, and which is just picking a tool?

options.label: "Vendor B's OCR accuracy looked best in the demo — go with them."

"Before any of these help, I want to spend two days mapping how a verification request actually moves through your front desk right now — the demos all assume clean, single-format insurer replies, and I don't yet know if that's true here."
Both are equally useful — one is just faster

feedback.judgement: Right. The first response answers the question the client asked. The second answers the question they should have asked, and it's the only one that can be wrong in a useful way — if the mapping turns up a clean process, the vendor comparison becomes trivial and you say so.
feedback.tool-pick: This answers exactly what was asked, which is the trap. Rating OCR accuracy from a demo tells you nothing about whether OCR is the actual bottleneck at Larkspur — demos run on the vendor's cleanest sample documents, not on a decade of scanned faxes from forty different insurers.
feedback.both: They're not equivalent in cost of being wrong. Picking a tool from a demo and being wrong costs the client a contract and six months. Mapping the process first and being wrong costs two days, and you'll know it's wrong before anyone signs anything.

contentSections.concept: A tool recommendation answers "which product." A judgement call answers "what's actually happening, and does a product even belong in the answer." Clients ask for the first because it's the question they know how to ask — a vendor's sales page is written to be understood without a diagnosis. Your first job is noticing that the question underneath is different, and saying so before you're locked into comparing spec sheets.

contentSections.title: What judgement costs, and what it's worth

contentSections.body:
This isn't a purity position — clients do sometimes need a tool recommendation, and there's nothing wrong with giving one once you've earned the right to. The problem is giving one *first*, because a tool recommendation made before a diagnosis is a guess wearing a consultant's invoice.

The honest version of "can you just tell us which one to buy" is: "I can, after I understand what's actually slowing your team down — otherwise I'm recommending against a guess at your process, not your actual process." That sentence is uncomfortable to say to someone who wants a fast answer. It is also the sentence that keeps you from being the person blamed when the tool doesn't fix anything, because the actual problem was never in scope.

contentSections.scenario: Six months after a different consultant recommended a document-classification tool for Larkspur's third location, the front desk still spends 20 minutes per patient on insurance verification — the same time as before the tool. The tool's own dashboard shows 94% classification accuracy.
contentSections.question: The tool is performing as sold. Why hasn't the 20 minutes moved?

options.label: The staff aren't trained on the new tool well enough
Classification accuracy was never the bottleneck — the 20 minutes was mostly waiting on insurer phone queues and re-keying denials, which the tool doesn't touch
94% accuracy is too low for this use case

feedback.wrong-target: Correct. A tool can hit its own metric perfectly and change nothing the client experiences, if the metric it optimises was never where the time went. Nobody mapped the 20 minutes before recommending anything, so the recommendation solved a problem that wasn't the client's actual problem.
feedback.training: Possible, but it's the second question, not the first. Before assuming a training gap, you'd want to know whether the tool was ever pointed at the actual bottleneck — and in this case the 94% accuracy figure tells you it was doing its job fine; the job just wasn't the constraint.
feedback.accuracy-too-low: 94% is a strong number for document classification in production. Chasing it higher wouldn't move the 20 minutes either, because classification speed was never what the 20 minutes was made of.

contentSections.mechanism: This is the failure mode of a tool recommendation made without a diagnosis: the tool gets judged, correctly, against its own spec, and the client's actual experience doesn't move — because the thing the tool was built to do and the thing that was actually costing time were never the same thing. Nobody checked before the purchase.

contentSections.body: The client is paying for the answer to "what's actually going on," even when what they ask for is "which one should we buy" — and confusing the two is the first mistake this job lets you make.

title: The three engagements: diagnose, design, deliver
description: The same client request can mean three different jobs. Naming which one before you scope it is what keeps you from being blamed for a deliverable nobody agreed to.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish diagnose, design, and deliver engagements by what each actually produces
Read a client's request for signals of which engagement they actually want

contentSections.title: Three different jobs wearing one name

contentSections.body: An email lands: "Hi — we'd like to hire someone to do an automation audit of our claims intake process." Sounds like one job. It's actually asking for one of three different things, and the sender may not know which.

**Diagnose** produces a written assessment: here's how the process actually runs, here's where the cost and time go, here's what's worth automating and what isn't — no build, no vendor selection, sometimes not even a specific tool recommendation. The deliverable is a document and a conversation.

**Design** produces a spec: given an agreed target (a specific step, a specific automation approach), here's exactly what it does, what data it touches, what happens when it's wrong, and what it costs to run — detailed enough that an engineering team could build from it without you in the room. The deliverable is a blueprint, still nothing running.

**Deliver** produces a working thing: the automation is built, tested against real cases, and handed over running. The deliverable is software in production.

The words a client uses — "audit," "assessment," "help us automate" — map onto all three inconsistently, because clients aren't required to know this taxonomy. You are.

contentSections.scenario: The claims-intake email continues: "...and if it makes sense, go ahead and build whatever you recommend. We don't want a report that sits in a drawer."
contentSections.question: Given that whole sentence, which engagement is actually being requested?

options.label: Diagnose only — "if it makes sense" means the decision to build comes later
All three in sequence, but the client hasn't separated them into phases yet — and won't, unless you do
Deliver — they said "go ahead and build"

feedback.sequence: Right. "If it makes sense" is a diagnose gate — they want the assessment first. "Go ahead and build whatever you recommend" is deliver intent stapled onto the same sentence, with design invisibly assumed to happen in between. Left alone, this becomes one invoice for three jobs with no checkpoint where either of you can stop, which is exactly the setup that produces scope disputes in month two.
feedback.diagnose-only: This reads only the first half of the sentence. "If it makes sense, go ahead and build" is explicit intent to continue past the diagnosis — they're not asking you to stop and hand over a report; they're asking you to keep going if the report says to.
feedback.deliver: This reads only the second half. "If it makes sense" is a real conditional, not a formality — it means there's a decision point before building starts, and that decision point is the diagnosis. Treating this as a pure build request skips the gate the client themselves put in the sentence.

contentSections.concept: Client language routinely bundles two or three engagements into one sentence, because from where they sit it's one goal ("fix the claims problem") rather than three deliverables. Naming the phases back to them — usually in the proposal, sometimes on the first call — turns an ambiguous ask into three decision points, each with its own scope and its own invoice, and each a place either of you can stop without it reading as a failure.

contentSections.title: Why the mismatch costs you specifically

contentSections.body: A diagnose engagement scoped and priced as a diagnose engagement, then delivered as a diagnose engagement, will still get read by the client as a failure if what they actually wanted — without saying so — was deliver. The mismatch doesn't show up in your scope document. It shows up in their face when you hand over a report and they ask, "okay, so when does the building start?"

contentSections.scenario: You're scoping a new engagement. Before you write the proposal, you're trying to work out which of the three the client actually wants — not just what they said.
contentSections.question: Select every signal that genuinely tells you which engagement is being requested.

items.label: Whether the budget conversation mentions a build phase or stops at "assessment"
Whether they mention having tried to build something like this before and it not working
Whether they have an internal engineering team who'd expect to receive a spec rather than watch you build
Whether the email uses the word "urgent"
How long the initial email is
Whether the person emailing you has budget authority to approve a build, or only an assessment

explanation.budget-shape: Real signal. A budget that stops after a fixed assessment fee, with no mention of a follow-on number, is telling you diagnose is the actual engagement even if the email said "help us automate."
explanation.prior-attempts: Real signal. A client who's already tried to build something and had it fail is usually asking for design or diagnose this time, even if they don't say so — they want someone to get the plan right before anyone builds again.
explanation.internal-eng: Real signal, and an important one. If they have an engineering team, "deliver" often isn't even on the table — they want design, a spec their own team can build from, and hiring you to also build it would be a duplicate cost they didn't ask for.
explanation.urgency-language: Not a signal for which engagement — "urgent" tells you about timeline pressure, not about whether they want a report, a spec, or working software. All three can be urgent.
explanation.email-length: Not a signal. A three-line email and a three-paragraph email can both be asking for the same engagement; length tracks how much the sender likes writing, not what they need.
explanation.who-signs: Real signal, and the one worth confirming directly if the others are ambiguous. Someone with authority to approve a diagnostic fee but not a build budget is telling you, structurally, that deliver isn't happening this round regardless of what the email implied.

contentSections.synthesis: Three real signals and two decoys. The decoys share a property worth noticing: they're about how the request was written, not what it was actually asking for. Tone and length are easy to read and tell you almost nothing about scope.

contentSections.body: Diagnose, design, and deliver are three different deliverables, three different price tags, and three different ways to disappoint a client who wanted a different one — name which you're doing before you start, out loud, in writing.

title: Why most automation projects fail on the process, not the technology
description: A working model can still fail in production, because the thing it automates was never consistent enough to automate — and the automation just makes that inconsistency faster and harder to see.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose whether an automation failure originates in the model or in the process feeding it
Identify process signals that predict an automation project will fail before any model is built

contentSections.title: The model worked. Nothing got better.

contentSections.body:
A regional logistics company, Northbeam Freight, installs an AI system that reads incoming vendor invoices and auto-files them against purchase orders. The vendor's benchmark accuracy: 96%. Six months later, 40% of invoices still land in a human review queue.

Nobody's model got worse. What happened is upstream: three different warehouses enter the same vendor's name three different ways — "Acme Corp," "ACME Corporation LLC," "Acme Corp. (Denver)." The model reads the invoice correctly every time. It just can't match "Acme Corp" to a purchase order filed under "ACME Corporation LLC," because nothing upstream ever decided those are the same vendor.

This is the single most common failure shape in this work, and it's worth naming precisely because it doesn't look like a technology failure — it looks like one, gets diagnosed as one, and gets "fixed" with a bigger model or more training data, which does nothing, because the inconsistency isn't in what the model has to read. It's in what the three warehouses agreed to call the same thing, which is nothing.

Automation doesn't fix process inconsistency. It **hardens** it — it takes a mess that a person could route around by recognizing "oh, that's Acme again" on sight, and turns it into a mess a system will confidently mismatch every time, at scale, faster than anyone catches it.

contentSections.scenario: The Northbeam invoice-matching system has 96% read accuracy on the document itself, and a 40% human-review rate on the overall process.
contentSections.question: Where does the 40% actually come from, given that the read accuracy is high?

options.label: The model's 96% accuracy is being measured wrong — it must be lower in practice

The model correctly reads what's on the invoice; the failure is matching that correct read against inconsistent vendor names in the purchase-order system, which is a data-standards gap the model can't close
The model needs more training examples of invoices from these specific warehouses

feedback.matching-gap: Correct. The two numbers aren't measuring the same thing: 96% is read accuracy on the document, 40% review rate is a downstream matching failure against inconsistent reference data. More training data teaches the model to read invoices better, which it already does — it can't teach the model that "Acme Corp" and "ACME Corporation LLC" refer to the same vendor, because that fact doesn't exist anywhere it can learn it from.
feedback.measurement-wrong: The two figures aren't in tension — they're measuring different steps. 96% read accuracy can be entirely correct and true, and still coexist with a 40% downstream match failure, because reading the invoice and matching it to the right purchase order are two separate operations, and only the first one improved.
feedback.more-training: More training data on invoice reading would push read accuracy up from an already-high 96% toward some ceiling — it does nothing about a vendor-naming inconsistency that lives in the purchase-order system, not in the invoices. This is the expensive version of the mistake: spending model-improvement budget on a step that was never broken.

contentSections.mechanism: The failure sits at the seam between two systems that were never made to agree on a shared vocabulary — here, what counts as "the same vendor." No amount of model quality closes a seam like that, because the seam isn't a modelling problem. It's a decision nobody made: which of "Acme Corp," "ACME Corporation LLC," and "Acme Corp. (Denver)" is canonical, and who's responsible for keeping new entries consistent with it. Until someone makes that decision — a person, a rule, a lookup table — the automation will keep hitting the same wall at the same rate, however good the model gets.

contentSections.title: Reading the warning signs before you build anything

contentSections.problem: Before recommending automation for Northbeam's invoice matching, you're asked to write a short pre-mortem: what process conditions, if they exist, predict this project fails the way it did — regardless of which vendor's model gets used.

steps.label: Check whether the input has one canonical form or many
steps.work: Vendor names come from three warehouses' separate data entry, with no shared master list. Same real-world vendor, three different strings in the system.
steps.why: This is the single strongest predictor. If the same real-world thing can legitimately be represented three different ways in the data the automation reads, no model — however accurate at reading — closes that gap, because the gap isn't in the reading.

steps.label: Check who currently resolves the inconsistency, and how
steps.work: Right now, a human in accounts payable recognizes "oh, that's Acme again" by memory and institutional knowledge, and manually reconciles it. That knowledge exists in one person's head, not in any system.
steps.why: This tells you what the automation is actually replacing: not a mechanical lookup, but a person's tacit pattern-matching. Automating the mechanical part while leaving the tacit part unaddressed is exactly how you get a 96%-accurate reader stuck at 40% review.

steps.label: Ask whether fixing the input is in scope, or only reading it
steps.work: The brief as given is "automate invoice matching." Nobody has proposed a master vendor list or a data-entry standard across the three warehouses.
steps.why: If cleaning the input is out of scope, the honest projection is that automation will hit roughly the same wall the human currently routes around by memory — which is worth saying before the build starts, not after.

steps.label: State the actual recommendation
steps.work: Recommend a master vendor-name lookup (a genuinely small, unglamorous piece of work) before or alongside the matching automation — not instead of it, but as the thing that determines whether the matching automation can ever clear more than roughly 60% of invoices without review.
steps.why: This is the sentence that makes the pre-mortem worth writing. It reframes "which AI tool should we buy" into "fix this first, or the AI tool inherits this exact ceiling."

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. A staffing agency, Vantage Staffing, wants to automate matching timesheet hours to client invoices. Timesheets are submitted through five different formats depending on which client portal a recruiter used that week — some CSV, some PDF scans, some a client's own web form with no export at all.

blanks.prompt: What's the single strongest predictor of failure here, in one phrase?
blanks.why: Same pattern as Northbeam: the thing feeding the automation doesn't have one consistent shape, so the automation inherits the inconsistency instead of resolving it.

blanks.prompt: Who currently resolves this inconsistency, and how? (one sentence)
blanks.answer: a recruiter or coordinator manually re-keys or reformats each timesheet by hand before invoicing
blanks.why: Naming the current human workaround tells you what tacit knowledge the automation would need to replace — here, recognizing which of five formats arrived and handling each one, which is exactly the kind of judgement a document-reading model isn't given unless someone tells it there are five formats to expect.

blanks.prompt: Is fixing the input in scope, based on the brief as given? (yes/no, one sentence why)
blanks.answer: no, the brief only asks to automate the matching step, not to standardize timesheet submission
accept: no — only the matching step was mentioned
blanks.why: Same gap as Northbeam. Naming it explicitly, before scoping the build, is what turns this into a conversation the client can make an informed decision about instead of a surprise at the review-rate metric six months in.

blanks.prompt: What's the actual recommendation? (one sentence)
blanks.answer: standardize timesheet submission to a single format, or build a per-format ingestion step, before or alongside the matching automation
accept: fix input formats first, then automate matching
blanks.why: The recommendation names the real constraint the client is buying their way out of, rather than letting "automate the matching" quietly promise more than it can deliver against five incompatible formats.

contentSections.procedure: **Canonical form? → who resolves it now, and how? → is fixing the input in scope? → recommend accordingly.** Run this before recommending any automation, because every one of these questions is cheap to ask and expensive to skip.

contentSections.body: A model can hit its own benchmark and change nothing the client experiences — check whether the process feeding it has one consistent shape before you recommend anything that reads it.

title: What you own when it goes wrong
description: A recommendation that goes live and then causes harm splits responsibility between what you scoped and warned about, and what the client did with it — and that split has to be drawn before anything goes live, not argued about after.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish consultant accountability from client accountability when an automated recommendation fails in production
Identify what a scope document and risk disclosure need to state to make that split defensible later

contentSections.title: "Was this the model or was this us?"

contentSections.body: Three weeks after your recommended intake-classification system goes live at a mid-size clinic network, a patient's message describing chest pain gets auto-routed to the general-inquiries queue instead of the urgent-triage queue. The callback goes out three days late. Nobody is physically hurt, but it's close enough that the clinic's operations director calls you directly: "Was this the model, or was this us?"

That question has a real answer, and it isn't "it's complicated" — it's a specific division of labour that should have been written down before the system went live.

**What you own:** the recommendation itself, including its stated limits. If you recommended a classifier without flagging that it hadn't been tested on symptom descriptions using non-standard phrasing, and it then misroutes exactly that kind of message, that's on your risk disclosure, or the lack of one.

**What the client owns:** how they operate what you handed over. If your scope explicitly said "this system should not be the sole gate on anything time-sensitive — pair it with a human spot-check on ambiguous cases," and they turned that off to save headcount, the failure happened downstream of your recommendation, in a decision you didn't make and, if you did your job, warned against in writing.

The two owners aren't always cleanly separable. But the line exists, and where it falls depends entirely on what got written down before launch — not on how sympathetic either side sounds after.

contentSections.title: The clinic's operations director wants an answer
contentSections.opening: Your original scope document, which the operations director signed, includes this line under "Limitations": *"The classifier has not been validated against non-standard symptom phrasing (e.g. regional or informal language for urgent symptoms) and should not operate without a human reviewing messages flagged below 85% confidence."* You've just learned the clinic disabled the human-review step two weeks ago to reduce a backlog, without telling you.

call.situation: The operations director is on the phone, audibly rattled, asking whether this is the model's fault or theirs.
call.question: What do you say first?

choices.label: "This is exactly why we scoped a human review step — you turned it off."
choices.consequence: Technically accurate and it lands as an attack on someone who's scared and looking for a way to understand what happened, not a fight. The conversation gets defensive fast, and you've spent your credibility on being right first.

choices.label: "That's on us — we'll review the model and get back to you."
choices.consequence: This is generous, and it's also false: it misstates what actually happened, which was a documented limitation the client disabled without notice. It protects the relationship for one phone call and creates a much worse conversation later if the true cause surfaces — for instance if the clinic's insurer asks for the incident timeline.

choices.label: "Let's walk through what happened together, starting with the confidence score on that specific message."
choices.consequence: You pull the specific case. The confidence score was 71% — below the 85% threshold that should have triggered human review. You ask, factually and without accusation, whether the review step was active that week.

confirm.situation: The director confirms the review step was disabled two weeks ago to clear a backlog, and admits nobody flagged the change back to you.
confirm.question: How do you close this?

choices.label: State plainly that this falls outside your recommendation as scoped, and leave it there
choices.consequence: Correct on the facts, and it stops one exchange short of useful. The director now knows whose fault it was and still has no idea how to prevent the next one — which they will remember about you.

choices.label: Confirm the review step was the safeguard for exactly this case, and propose a concrete fix — an alert when confidence-gated review gets disabled, not just a warning in a document
choices.consequence: You name what happened plainly, without either taking blame that isn't yours or leaving the director with nothing but the diagnosis. You also notice your own gap: a limitation written into a document nobody re-reads under backlog pressure isn't a safeguard, it's a sentence. You propose something that fails loudly instead.

defensive.summary: You were right and it didn't help. The director spent the rest of the call defending the decision instead of hearing you, and the relationship took a hit that had nothing to do with who was actually responsible.
defensive.lesson: Being correct about accountability and delivering that correctness well are two different skills, and the second one is what determines whether the client stays a client.

false-own.summary: The call ends warmly. Three weeks later, the clinic's own incident review turns up the disabled safeguard, and now you've admitted fault for something you didn't cause, on the record, in a way that's awkward to walk back and looks worse than the truth would have.
false-own.lesson: Owning something you didn't cause isn't generosity — it's a version of the truth that doesn't survive someone else checking.

correct-but-cold.summary: The facts are established cleanly and correctly. The director gets off the call knowing it wasn't your fault and with no better plan than "remember to keep the review step on," which is exactly the kind of plan that fails again under the next backlog.
correct-but-cold.lesson: Correctly assigning fault is necessary and not sufficient — a client who just got hurt by their own process needs the next failure mode closed, not just this one named.

system-fix.summary: The director understands what happened, agrees the disabled safeguard was the proximate cause, and leaves with something concrete — an alert on the review step being disabled — instead of just a post-mortem. Your own gap (a written limitation nobody re-reads) gets closed too.
system-fix.lesson: The line between what you own and what the client owns is real, and stating it well means pairing it with something that prevents the next version of the same failure — including fixing the parts of your own scope that turned out to be too easy to quietly ignore.

contentSections.body: The line between what you own and what the client owns gets drawn by what's written down before launch, not by how the conversation goes after something breaks — and a limitation that's only a sentence in a document isn't actually a safeguard.

title: Working this job at variable capacity
description: Which parts of a consulting engagement genuinely need a live call on a good day, and which can be done async on any day — because assuming every stage needs a synchronous meeting is what makes this job impossible to sustain on a body that doesn't guarantee good days.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish engagement stages that require synchronous, high-energy interaction from ones that can be done async at variable capacity

contentSections.title: Not every stage costs the same

contentSections.body: Tuesday: three client calls scheduled, a process-mapping session, and a proposal due. Tuesday also turns out to be a day where standing up for more than ten minutes brings on presyncope, and the idea of holding a coherent thought through a 45-minute stakeholder call is not realistic. The work doesn't stop existing. What changes is which pieces of it get done today, and which get moved to a version of the work that doesn't require a live call.

A consulting engagement isn't one uniform activity — it's a sequence of stages with genuinely different demands. A live stakeholder interview needs real-time listening, follow-up questions, and reading tone, which costs differently than reviewing a document at your own pace. Drafting a scope document needs sustained focus but not another person's calendar. Reading through a week of ticket logs to estimate a baseline can be done in five-minute stretches between rests.

The useful move isn't "push through" or "cancel everything." It's knowing, ahead of a bad day, which stages of the work you're currently in have an async version — because building that flexibility into how you scope and run engagements, before you need it, is what keeps a bad day from becoming a missed deliverable.

contentSections.scenario: A four-stage engagement is underway: (1) a live kickoff interview with the client's ops lead, (2) reviewing two weeks of exported ticket data to build a baseline, (3) a working session drawing the process map with the team present, (4) writing the final recommendation document.
contentSections.question: Select the stages that have a genuine async alternative — one that produces comparably useful work, not just a lower-effort version.

items.label: The live kickoff interview
Reviewing the exported ticket data
The live process-mapping working session
Writing the final recommendation document

explanation.kickoff: No genuine async substitute. A first interview relies on follow-up questions in the moment — noticing a hedge in someone's answer and asking about it right then is exactly the thing an emailed questionnaire can't replicate; that's covered in more depth once you get to the interviewing phase of this track. This stage should be scheduled for a day you can actually show up present for it, or split into a shorter version.
explanation.ticket-review: Genuinely async. Reading exported data at your own pace, in whatever short stretches a bad day allows, produces the same baseline as reading it in one sitting — the work doesn't degrade by being spread across five fifteen-minute sessions instead of one seventy-five-minute one.
explanation.mapping-session: No genuine async substitute, for the same reason as the kickoff — the value of drawing the map with the team present is that they correct it live, in the room, which is covered later in this phase. A version done alone from notes and then emailed for corrections is real work, but it's a different, weaker version, not an equivalent one.
explanation.final-doc: Genuinely async. Writing doesn't require anyone else's calendar and can be done in whatever increments the day allows, reviewed and revised across sessions without losing quality.

contentSections.synthesis: Two of the four stages have a genuine async version; two don't, because their value specifically comes from real-time interaction with another person. The planning move is knowing this before you build a project timeline — scheduling the two synchronous stages for whichever slots in the week are most likely to be workable, and treating the other two as flexible reserve you can shift a bad day's work into.

contentSections.body: One more piece: this isn't only about protecting your own capacity — a client whose stated timeline assumes every week is a good week is setting an engagement up to look late even when the actual work is on track. Scoping in explicit buffer, and naming upfront which stages need a synchronous slot versus which can flex, is a professional practice, not a disclosure of anything personal. "Interviews are scheduled with a two-day flex window either side" reads as competent project management to a client. It also happens to be exactly the structure that makes the job survivable.
Sort an engagement's stages into synchronous and async before you need to, on a good day — so a bad day has somewhere real to put its hours instead of just falling behind.

learningObjectives.text: Classify client requests by the engagement type they actually require
Apply the accountability and process-diagnosis distinctions from this module to new scenarios

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing is timed, and the set doesn't expire — do all eight now or split them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Write Your Own Engagement One-Pager
description: Produce the document a prospective client reads before their first call: what you do, what you explicitly don't do, and what they get at each stage.

learningObjectives.text: Articulate your own consulting scope clearly enough for a client to self-select correctly
Apply the diagnose/design/deliver distinction to describe your own practice honestly

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every consultant who's been doing this for a while has an answer, even if unwritten, to "what exactly do you do?" Writing it down first, before a client asks, is what turns a fumbled explanation on a sales call into a document you send ahead of one — and it forces you to decide, in writing, which of the three engagements you're actually good at and willing to sell.

contentSections.title: Your engagement one-pager
contentSections.brief: A prospective client emails: "Can you send something explaining what working with you actually looks like?" This is the document you send back. It has to be short, specific, and honest about the limits of what you do — the kind of document that gets you a client who wants exactly what you offer, and correctly filters out one who doesn't.
contentSections.deliverable: A one-page description of what you do, what you don't, and what a client gets at each stage of working with you.

stages.title: Name which engagements you actually offer
stages.instructions: Using this module's diagnose/design/deliver taxonomy, decide which of the three you offer, and in what combination. It's fine to offer only diagnose and design, or all three — but write it as a real decision, not a default. If you'd only ever do deliver work alongside a partner engineering team, say that.
stages.checkpoint: You have one to three named engagements, each with a one-sentence description of what it produces.

stages.title: Write what you explicitly don't do
stages.instructions: Name at least two things you won't do, or won't do without conditions — for example, "I don't build and hand over automation without a written scope of what it should never be trusted to decide alone," echoing the accountability lesson in this module. This section is what makes the document trustworthy rather than promotional.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least two concrete exclusions, each specific enough that a client would know exactly what they're not getting.

stages.title: Describe what a client gets, stage by stage
stages.instructions: For each engagement you offer, write one or two sentences on what the client actually receives — a document, a spec, working software — and roughly what it costs them in time from both sides. Be concrete: "a two-week diagnosis producing a written assessment and a go/no-go recommendation" beats "a thorough analysis of your needs."
stages.checkpoint: Someone reading this could describe, in their own words, what they'd get and by when.

stages.title: Cut it to one page and self-check
stages.instructions: Cut it to a single page. Read it as the prospective client: does it tell you, in under two minutes, whether this consultant is the right fit for what you actually need? Then run the self-check below against your own draft.
stages.checkpoint: It fits on one page and contains no sentence that only sounds impressive without telling the reader something they could act on.

rubric.criterion: Engagement types are named using the module's taxonomy
rubric.meets: Uses diagnose/design/deliver (or explicitly reasoned equivalents) rather than vague language like "full-service automation consulting."

rubric.criterion: Exclusions are concrete, not generic humility
rubric.meets: Names specific things not done — a client could not do them by accident after reading this.

rubric.criterion: Deliverables are described in terms of what exists at the end
rubric.meets: Each engagement states what the client receives — a document, a spec, working software — not just an activity.

rubric.criterion: Judgement-versus-tool-pick is reflected somewhere in the document
rubric.meets: The document signals, explicitly or through its structure, that diagnosis precedes tool or build recommendations rather than skipping to them.

rubric.criterion: It reads as confident, not apologetic
rubric.meets: Limitations are stated as scope decisions, not as hedges or apologies.

rubric.criterion: It fits on one page
rubric.meets: A prospective client could read the whole thing in under two minutes and know whether to book a call.

contentSections.body: A client who reads this and books a call is a client who already knows roughly what they're buying — which is worth more, over a career, than a client won by promising everything.

title: Checkpoint — What the Work Involves
description: Ten questions pulling across the module. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — What the Work Involves

questions.from: This module — What the Work Involves
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a judgement call and a tool recommendation?

options.label: A judgement call diagnoses what's actually happening first; a tool pick answers 'which product' without checking
A judgement call is more expensive
They're the same thing at different stages of an engagement

questions.explanation: A tool recommendation made before a diagnosis is a guess wearing an invoice — the Northbeam invoice-matching case showed a tool hitting its own benchmark while changing nothing the client experienced, because nobody diagnosed the actual bottleneck first.

questions.from: This module — What the Work Involves
questions.prompt: A diagnose engagement's deliverable is:

options.label: Working software in production
A written assessment and recommendation, no build
A build-ready spec for someone else's engineering team

questions.explanation: Diagnose produces a document and a conversation — an assessment of what's happening and what's worth automating, without building or specifying anything.

questions.from: This module — What the Work Involves
questions.prompt: A client says "our dev team is ready to build, they just need to know exactly what." Which engagement do they need?

options.label: Diagnose
Design
Deliver

questions.explanation: Design produces the spec their own team executes — hiring you to also build it would be work they didn't ask for and didn't need.

questions.from: This module — What the Work Involves
questions.prompt: Why did the invoice-matching model at Northbeam hit 96% accuracy while the overall review rate stayed at 40%?

options.label: The model was measured incorrectly
The model read documents correctly but couldn't match inconsistent vendor names across three warehouses' data entry — a gap the model's own benchmark never measured
The model needed more training examples

questions.explanation: Automation doesn't fix process inconsistency, it hardens it — the model's benchmark measured reading accuracy, not the downstream matching failure against inconsistent reference data.

questions.from: This module — What the Work Involves
questions.prompt: The pre-mortem procedure for spotting process risk before recommending automation starts with:

options.label: Checking whether the input has one canonical form or many
Picking the vendor with the best benchmark
Estimating the ROI

questions.explanation: Canonical form, then who resolves inconsistency now and how, then whether fixing the input is in scope, then the recommendation — in that order, because each later question depends on the answer to the one before it.

questions.from: This module — What the Work Involves
questions.prompt: In the clinic misrouting case, what actually determined the split between what the consultant owned and what the client owned?

options.label: How sympathetic each party sounded on the call
What was written down — the scoped limitation and risk disclosure — before the system went live
Whoever apologized first

questions.explanation: The line between consultant and client accountability gets drawn by what's written down before launch, not by how the after-the-fact conversation goes.

questions.from: This module — What the Work Involves
questions.prompt: Why was a written limitation clause not enough to actually prevent the clinic's misrouting failure?

options.label: The clause was inaccurate
A sentence in a document nobody re-reads under backlog pressure isn't a functioning safeguard — the fix needed to make the safeguard's status visible or alerting
The clause should have been longer

questions.explanation: A written limitation establishes accountability after a failure; it doesn't prevent the failure. Making the safeguard fail loudly — an alert when it's disabled — closes the actual gap.

questions.from: This module — What the Work Involves
questions.prompt: Which engagement stages in this module's example genuinely have no async substitute?

options.label: Reviewing exported data and writing the final document
The live kickoff interview and the live process-mapping working session
None — every stage of a consulting engagement can be done async

questions.explanation: Both rely on real-time interaction — follow-up questions in an interview, and the team correcting a map live in the room — that an emailed version can't equivalently replicate.

questions.from: This module — What the Work Involves
questions.prompt: What's the professional way to build bad-day flexibility into a client-facing project timeline?

options.label: Disclose your health situation directly so the client understands
Name fixed dates for the synchronous stages and a flexible range for the async ones, presented as normal project planning
Avoid committing to any dates at all

questions.explanation: Naming which dates are fixed and which are a range reads as competent project management to a client, discloses nothing personal, and happens to be exactly the structure that makes the job sustainable.

questions.from: This module — What the Work Involves
questions.prompt: A client's ambiguous request bundles "figure out why it's broken" and "just fix it" into one sentence. What's the right response?

options.label: Quote a single price covering everything, since that's what they asked for
Propose a phase break — a diagnosis first, with the fix scoped separately once the diagnosis is done
Assume they want deliver, since 'fix it' was mentioned

questions.explanation: Naming the phase break turns one unbounded ask into two decision points, which is what keeps an ambiguous request from becoming a scope dispute later.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: The documented process and the real one are different documents
description: Every workplace has an official process and a shadow process it actually runs on — and the shadow process is usually the one worth mapping.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish the documented process from the process actually in use
Recognise the concrete signals that a shadow process exists

contentSections.title: Two documents, one process

contentSections.body:
Larkspur Dental's employee handbook describes insurance prior-authorization in four steps: submit request, insurer reviews, insurer responds, front desk schedules. Clean, four boxes, one page.

The billing coordinator, Renata, actually works from a shared Google Sheet she built two years ago after step two kept silently stalling — it has fourteen columns, three of them for insurers she's learned always reject the first submission, and a column called "call again Thursday" that exists because Thursday is when one particular insurer's queue is shortest. Nobody put that sheet in the handbook. It's the process.

This isn't a story about Larkspur being disorganized — it's close to universal. A documented process is written once, by someone trying to describe the ideal case, and then the real world adds exceptions, workarounds, and tribal knowledge faster than anyone updates the document. The gap between the two isn't a failure to maintain documentation. It's evidence of everything the documented process didn't account for.

That gap is exactly what you're there to map. A process map built from the handbook describes a process that, in Renata's experience, doesn't exist. A process map built from the Google Sheet describes the one that runs Larkspur's actual patient scheduling — including the parts nobody would think to write down because they're so routine to the person doing them that they don't register as noteworthy.

contentSections.scenario: You ask Larkspur's practice owner for "the process for insurance verification," and he hands you a one-page PDF from the practice management software vendor: four boxes, a clean flow. Separately, you notice Renata has a browser tab permanently open to a spreadsheet titled "insurer notes — DO NOT DELETE."
contentSections.question: Which one is the process you should map first?

options.label: The PDF — it's the official documented process
The spreadsheet — it's clearly where the actual working knowledge lives, and the PDF is what someone believes happens, not what happens
Neither — start from a blank whiteboard and build the map from scratch in the interview

feedback.spreadsheet: Right instinct — though "map first" doesn't mean map only. The spreadsheet is the strongest available signal of where the real process diverges from the documented one, and "DO NOT DELETE" tells you exactly how load-bearing it's become. You'll still validate the PDF's structure against it, but you're not starting from the fiction.
feedback.pdf: This is the trap. The PDF describes what the vendor's software is designed to support, or what someone wrote when the process was designed, not what fourteen columns of exception-handling in a spreadsheet tell you actually happens now. Mapping from the PDF alone produces a map that looks clean and describes nothing real.
feedback.blank: Starting from nothing wastes information that already exists — the spreadsheet is essentially a rough draft of the real process, written by the person who lives inside it every day. Ignoring it to start fresh means re-discovering, slowly, everything Renata already knows.

contentSections.concept: A documented process describes intent. A shadow process — the spreadsheet, the sticky notes, the personal email folder, the private Slack channel — describes what actually has to happen to get the work done given everything the documented process didn't anticipate. Neither one is "the truth" by itself: the documented version tells you what the organisation believes should happen, and the shadow version tells you what's actually keeping it running. Mapping starts by taking the shadow process seriously as data, not as a symptom of noncompliance.

contentSections.title: Spotting the shadow process before anyone tells you

contentSections.body: Nobody announces a shadow process in a kickoff meeting — mentioning it can feel like admitting the official system doesn't work, which people are often reluctant to say to an outside consultant on day one. So the useful skill is recognising the signals before anyone tells you directly: a personal spreadsheet with a possessive or defensive title, a sticky note taped to a monitor, a printed cheat sheet nobody officially issued, a Slack channel named after a person instead of a process, a phrase like "oh, I just remember which ones do that."

contentSections.scenario: You're doing a walkthrough of Larkspur's front desk on day one, before any formal interviews. You're watching for signals of a shadow process, not asking about one yet.
contentSections.question: Select every signal below that's a genuine sign of a shadow process, worth following up on.

items.label: A row of sticky notes on the monitor listing which insurers to call before 10am
A personal spreadsheet, not linked from the practice management software, tracking insurer quirks
A staff member saying "I just kind of know which ones to double-check" when asked how they verify a submission
A desk with no visible paper or sticky notes at all
A staff member typing quickly and confidently through the software
A shared drive folder named "insurer cheat sheets" that isn't referenced anywhere in the official handbook

explanation.sticky-notes: Genuine signal. Physical reminders outside any official system are one of the most visible tells — someone decided the official process didn't hold this information reliably enough, so they externalised it themselves.
explanation.personal-sheet: Genuine signal, and often the richest one — a personal tracking sheet is usually months or years of accumulated exception-handling knowledge in one place.
explanation.hedge-phrase: Genuine signal. "I just kind of know" describes tacit knowledge that exists nowhere except in that person's head — which is exactly the knowledge a process map needs to surface, because it disappears the day they leave.
explanation.clean-desk: Not a signal either way — a clean desk tells you about someone's workspace habits, not about whether tacit process knowledge exists. Plenty of shadow knowledge lives entirely in someone's head or in a digital file, leaving the physical desk clean.
explanation.fast-typing: Not a signal either way — confidence and speed are consistent with either a well-designed official process or a well-rehearsed workaround. You can't tell which from watching hands move.
explanation.shared-folder: Genuine signal. A folder that exists and gets used but appears nowhere in official documentation is exactly the gap between the two documents this lesson is about.

contentSections.synthesis: Four real signals and two decoys. The decoys share a property: they describe how someone works, not what knowledge they're drawing on — and it's the knowledge, not the working style, that tells you a shadow process exists.

contentSections.body: The handbook tells you what the organisation believes happens. The spreadsheet nobody officially sanctioned tells you what actually keeps the work running — map from the second one, and use the first one to see the gap.

title: Following one item all the way through
description: Pick a single real request and trace it from the moment it enters the process to the moment it leaves — the technique that turns a vague sense of 'it takes a while' into an actual map.

learningObjectives.text: Trace a single unit of work through a process end to end, recording timestamps and handoffs

contentSections.title: One item, start to finish

contentSections.body: Instead of asking Renata to describe the prior-authorization process in the abstract, you ask her to pull up one specific request from last week — patient Maria D., a root canal referral needing prior authorization from her insurer — and walk you through exactly what happened to it, step by step, with times if she has them.

This is the single most reliable technique in process mapping: **follow one item, not the category.** Asking "how does prior-authorization work" invites a description of the ideal case, edited in real time to sound coherent. Asking "walk me through what happened to Maria D.'s referral, from the moment it arrived to the moment it was resolved" invites a memory, which is a different and much more honest kind of data — memories include the annoying wait, the phone call that went to voicemail twice, the moment someone forgot and had to be reminded.

The trace should record, for each step: what happened, roughly when, who touched it, and what they were waiting on before they could act. You're not asking for a polished summary. You're asking for the actual sequence of events, including the parts that make the process look bad.

contentSections.question: Renata's trace of Maria D.'s referral, once she reconstructs it, involves these events. Put them in the order they actually happened.
steps: Dentist's referral note is entered into the practice management system (Monday, 9:15am)
Renata submits the prior-auth request to the insurer via their online portal (Monday, 11:40am — batched with three other submissions)
No response by Wednesday; Renata calls the insurer and waits 35 minutes on hold before reaching someone
Insurer states the request is missing a specific clinical code and needs to be resubmitted
Renata resubmits with the correct code (Wednesday, 3:50pm)
Insurer approves the request (the following Monday)
Renata calls Maria to schedule the procedure
contentSections.explanation: Two things this trace surfaces that a description of the 'process' never would: the submission wasn't sent the moment it was entered — it sat until Renata had a batch of four to submit together, which is itself a real practice worth mapping. And the entire delay from Monday to the following Monday — six business days — came down to one missing clinical code that nobody caught until someone was on hold for 35 minutes to ask. Neither of those facts appears in a four-box flowchart. Both of them are where the actual time went.

contentSections.title: Doing the trace, and doing it again

contentSections.problem: Turn Maria D.'s trace into a usable process-map fragment: a short table of steps, actors, and elapsed time between them, ready to feed into the fuller map later in this module.

steps.label: List the discrete steps in order
steps.work: 1. Referral entered. 2. Batched submission to insurer. 3. Follow-up call after no response. 4. Resubmission with corrected code. 5. Approval. 6. Patient scheduled.
steps.why: A discrete step is one identifiable action by one actor. "Renata handled the insurance stuff" is not a step; "Renata submitted the request" and "Renata called to follow up" are two different steps with two different durations.

steps.label: Record elapsed time between each pair of steps, not just total time
steps.work: Referral entered → submission: 2h25m (batching delay). Submission → follow-up call: ~2 days (waiting on the insurer). Call → resubmission: same day, a few hours. Resubmission → approval: ~5 days.
steps.why: Total time (6 business days) tells you the process is slow. The gaps between steps tell you *where* — here, two long waits (batching, and the insurer's silent review period) dwarf everything Renata actually did herself, which took under an hour of active work across the whole thing.

steps.label: Note who's waiting on whom at each gap
steps.work: The batching delay: Maria is waiting on Renata's internal batching habit. The insurer silence: Renata (and Maria) are waiting on the insurer, with no visibility into their queue. The resubmission-to-approval gap: same, waiting on the insurer again.
steps.why: This is the fact that determines what's even automatable. Batching is Renata's own workflow choice — potentially changeable. The insurer's review time is external and outside anyone at Larkspur's control — a fact to plan around, not a bug to fix.

steps.label: Flag anything that looks like a workaround or a near-miss
steps.work: The missing clinical code wasn't caught until a 35-minute hold call — a near-miss that, if Renata hadn't happened to catch it during that call, could have sat silently for another week.
steps.why: Near-misses are the clearest signal of where a check is missing. This one points directly at a possible fix: validating the clinical code is present before submission, not after a week of silence.

faded.problem: Second trace, same procedure. A patient's routine cleaning appointment reminder: text reminder sent 48 hours before (Monday 8am for a Wednesday 8am appointment), patient doesn't confirm, a second reminder is sent 24 hours before (Tuesday 8am), still no confirmation, front desk calls the patient Tuesday at 4pm and reaches voicemail, patient shows up Wednesday as scheduled anyway.

blanks.prompt: How many discrete steps are in this trace?
blanks.why: First text reminder, second text reminder, phone call attempt, and the appointment itself — four identifiable actions, even though the outcome (patient shows up) required none of the follow-up to actually succeed.

blanks.prompt: What's the elapsed time between the two text reminders?
blanks.why: Monday 8am to Tuesday 8am — the gap between the two automated reminders, which is the one interval in this trace that was actually designed rather than accidental.

blanks.prompt: Who was the front desk waiting on when they made the Tuesday 4pm call, and what were they trying to resolve?
blanks.answer: waiting on the patient to confirm, trying to resolve whether the patient still intended to show up
blanks.why: Naming what a step is actually resolving — not just "calling the patient" — is what makes a trace useful later. Here it reveals the call accomplished nothing (voicemail), and the patient showed up anyway, which raises a real question about whether the call step adds value at all.

blanks.prompt: What's the near-miss or workaround-worth-flagging in this trace?
blanks.answer: the call reached voicemail and resolved nothing, yet the outcome was fine anyway — suggesting the call step may not be doing useful work
accept: the phone call was unnecessary since the patient showed up regardless
the call didn't actually confirm anything but nothing went wrong
blanks.why: This is a different kind of finding than Maria D.'s missing code — not a near-disaster, but a step that consumed staff time and phone-tag effort while contributing nothing to the actual outcome. That's just as worth flagging: not every finding from a trace is 'this nearly broke,' some are 'this may not be needed.'

contentSections.procedure: **List discrete steps → record elapsed time between each pair → name who's waiting on whom → flag near-misses and steps that add nothing.** Do this with two or three real traced items before drawing any map — one trace can be an outlier; two or three start to show you the pattern.

contentSections.body: "How does the process work" gets you a polished description. "Walk me through what happened to this exact request" gets you the truth, including the parts that make the process look bad — which are exactly the parts worth mapping.

title: Handoffs, queues and the waiting nobody measures
description: Most of a process's total time isn't anyone doing anything — it's a request sitting in a queue between two people, and nobody counts that time because nobody's actively working during it.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish touch time from wait time in a mapped process
Identify where handoffs create unmeasured queue time

contentSections.title: The number everyone reports, and the number that's true

contentSections.body: Ask Larkspur's front desk how long insurance verification takes, and the answer is "about 20 minutes." That's the time someone spends actively keying data and making calls. Maria D.'s referral, traced end to end in the last lesson, actually took six business days from entry to approval. Both numbers are honest. They're measuring completely different things.

**Touch time** is how long a human is actively working on something — typing, talking, deciding. **Wait time** is everything else: sitting in a queue, waiting for a reply, waiting for someone to notice it exists. When someone estimates "how long does X take," they almost always report touch time, because touch time is what they experience as work. Wait time doesn't feel like anything to the person waiting on someone else to act — it just feels like the task is quietly not moving.

In most administrative processes, wait time dwarfs touch time — often by a factor of ten or more. Which means the single highest-leverage question in process mapping isn't "how can we make the work faster" — it's "where is this thing sitting, doing nothing, while someone assumes it's being handled."

contentSections.scenario: Larkspur's own back-of-envelope claim is that a prior-authorization request takes about 20 minutes of staff time. Based on Maria D.'s traced timeline (six business days from entry to approval), estimate: roughly what percentage of that total elapsed time was actual touch time versus queue/wait time?
contentSections.question: What percentage of the total elapsed time was touch time?
contentSections.explanation: Roughly 20 minutes of active work out of six business days (about 2,880 minutes of business hours, or even just counting the roughly 48 elapsed hours across the relevant window) puts touch time at somewhere around 3-5% of total elapsed time. The rest — the batching delay, the two-day insurer silence, the 35-minute hold call, the resubmission wait — is queue and wait time nobody was actively working during. This is the pattern, not an outlier: in most administrative processes, the visible 'work' is a thin sliver on top of a much larger block of waiting that nobody names because nobody's doing anything visible during it.

contentSections.title: Finding the hidden handoff

contentSections.scenario: A separate Larkspur location reports that specialist referrals are "stuck for days" with no clear reason. You trace one: the dentist writes the referral note in the patient's chart on Monday. It's not visible to the front desk's referral queue until someone manually copies it into a separate referral-tracking spreadsheet — which happens whenever the office manager gets to it, sometimes same day, sometimes Thursday.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism causing the multi-day stall?

options.label: The dentist is too slow to write referral notes

There's an invisible handoff between two systems — the patient chart and the referral spreadsheet — that depends on one person noticing and manually transferring the information, with no trigger or deadline attached
The front desk isn't checking the referral queue often enough

feedback.invisible-handoff: Correct. The referral genuinely exists and is genuinely correct from the moment the dentist writes it — the stall isn't in anyone's competence, it's in an unmanaged handoff between two systems that nothing connects except one person's discretion about when to do the manual copy. Nobody owns making that transfer happen promptly, so it happens whenever it happens.
feedback.dentist-slow: The trace doesn't support this — the referral note itself is written promptly on Monday. The delay happens entirely after that, in getting the information from where it was written to where the front desk can see it.
feedback.front-desk-slow: The front desk is checking their queue fine — the problem is that the referral isn't *in* the queue yet, because it hasn't been manually copied over. Blaming the front desk targets the wrong side of the handoff; they can't act on information they don't have visibility into.

contentSections.mechanism: This is what an invisible handoff looks like in a map: two systems that should be connected are connected only by a person remembering to bridge them, with no deadline, no notification, and no consequence for delay. It doesn't show up as anyone doing anything wrong — everyone involved would say they're doing their job correctly. It shows up only when you trace one item and notice the multi-day gap between 'written' and 'visible to the next person who needs to act on it,' which is exactly the kind of gap a wait-time question surfaces and a touch-time question never asks about.

contentSections.body: When someone tells you how long something takes, they're almost always telling you the touch time — ask separately, explicitly, where it sits waiting, because that's usually where most of the real time is.

title: Drawing a map people will correct rather than nod at
description: A map presented as a finished, polished artefact gets nodded at in the room and quietly disputed afterward. A map built to be corrected gets fixed while you're still there.

learningObjectives.text: Design a map-review process that invites correction rather than agreement
Recognise structural flaws in a process map that obscure rather than reveal the real process

contentSections.title: Why the beautiful flowchart was wrong

contentSections.body: A different consultant, brought in before you, presented Larkspur's front-desk team with a polished flowchart of the referral process — clean boxes, a legend, arrows in three colours. Everyone in the room nodded. Two weeks later, the office manager mentioned offhand that the map had never matched Thursdays, because Thursday is when the practice runs a half-day and two of the boxes simply don't apply. Nobody had said anything in the meeting.

A finished-looking artefact invites agreement, not correction — contradicting something that already looks authoritative, in a room, out loud, to someone being paid to be right, is socially expensive. Most people won't pay that cost for a Thursday exception. They'll nod, and the map stays wrong.

The fix isn't a better flowchart. It's a different kind of session: draw the map live, visibly incomplete, using the team's own words as you go, and explicitly invite contradiction as the point of the exercise rather than a failure of it — "tell me where this is wrong" instead of "does this look right." A map that looks unfinished is psychologically easier to correct than one that looks done, because correcting it doesn't read as an attack on finished work.

contentSections.intro: Assemble the elements of a map-review session designed to get corrected, not nodded at. Three decisions.

fields.prompt: What state should the map be in when you show it to the team?

options.label: Fully polished and finished, so it looks credible
Visibly draft — rough boxes, hand-drawn or clearly editable, built live where possible
Not shown at all — just described verbally

feedback.draft: Right. A visibly unfinished artefact signals that correction is expected and welcome — it lowers the social cost of saying "actually, that's not right" because you're not contradicting something that already looks done.
feedback.polished: This is exactly what went wrong with the previous consultant's flowchart — polish signals completeness, and completeness invites nodding rather than correction, even when the map is wrong.
feedback.verbal-only: A verbal description with nothing to point at makes correction harder, not easier — there's no shared object for someone to say "no, right there, that box" about. A visible artefact, even a rough one, gives people something concrete to react to.

fields.prompt: What do you say when you show it to them?

options.label: "Does this look right to you?"
"Tell me everywhere this is wrong — I'd rather find out now than after we build something on top of it."
"Any questions?"

feedback.tell-me-wrong: Right. This makes correction the explicit goal of the exercise, states a real stake (building on a wrong map costs more later), and gives permission to disagree rather than requiring someone to volunteer disagreement unprompted.
feedback.does-it-look-right: This invites a yes/no answer, and "looks right" is a low bar — something can look plausible in five seconds of glancing at it and still be wrong about Thursdays. It doesn't prompt anyone to actually check it against their own experience.
feedback.any-questions: This invites questions, not corrections — and most people in a room don't have a 'question' about something being wrong, they have an objection, which feels different and riskier to voice unprompted.

fields.prompt: Whose language should label the steps on the map?

options.label: Formal process terminology, for professionalism
The words the team actually uses for each step, even if informal
Generic labels like "Step 1," "Step 2" to stay neutral

feedback.their-words: Right. If Renata calls it "the Thursday problem" or "the resubmit dance," using her own phrase on the map does two things: it signals the map was actually built from what she said, not translated into consultant-speak, and it makes errors easier to spot — a mislabeled step in her own vocabulary looks obviously wrong to her in a way a formal label might not.
feedback.formal: Formal terminology can obscure exactly the exceptions and workarounds that matter most — "prior authorization resubmission workflow" reads as authoritative and hides the specific, informal reality ("the resubmit dance") that Renata would immediately flag as wrong or missing if it were named plainly.
feedback.generic: Generic labels are neutral in the wrong way — they make the map easy to build and hard to check, because nobody can tell at a glance whether "Step 3" correctly represents what they actually do.

contentSections.synthesis: Draft-looking, explicitly inviting contradiction, in the team's own words — all three decisions point the same direction: make correction the path of least resistance, not the path of social risk. A map that gets fixed live, in the room, is worth more than one that gets nodded at and quietly wrong for months.

contentSections.title: The flaw that hides in a finished-looking map

contentSections.code:
Larkspur Referral Process — v1
