Legend: single path, no branches shown.
contentSections.question: This map was presented in a meeting and everyone nodded. Based on what you know about Maria D.'s traced referral, what's the flaw?

options.label: It's missing a box for the dentist's initial diagnosis

It shows a single straight-through path with no branch for what happens when the insurer rejects the first submission — which is exactly what happened to Maria D. and, per Renata's spreadsheet, happens routinely with specific insurers
The boxes should be numbered

feedback.no-branch: Correct. A single-path map with no rejection or resubmission branch describes the happy-path case only — the one case that, per Renata's own tracking, is not the routine one for several insurers. A map that omits the branch that actually happens most of the time for a meaningful share of cases isn't simplified, it's wrong.
feedback.missing-diagnosis: The dentist's diagnosis genuinely precedes this process but isn't really part of the referral workflow being mapped — this isn't the flaw that matters here, compared to omitting an entire branch that changes the outcome for real cases.
feedback.numbering: Cosmetic, and irrelevant to whether the map is accurate. A numbered version of the same single, incomplete path is exactly as wrong as this one.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A clean, single-path map is seductive precisely because it's easy to read and looks authoritative — and it's most dangerous exactly where the real process branches, because that's where a reader assumes the straight line continues to hold. The fix isn't to make the map more detailed everywhere; it's to add the branch at the one decision point (insurer approves vs. insurer rejects) that Maria D.'s trace and Renata's own spreadsheet both show is where the process actually diverges, and diverges often.

contentSections.body: A map that looks finished gets nodded at. A map that looks draft, invites contradiction by name, and uses the team's own words gets fixed while you're still in the room — which is the only place fixing it is cheap.

title: Exceptions: the 20% that consumes 80% of the effort
description: The happy path takes fifteen minutes. The exception path can take three weeks and eat most of a coordinator's actual working time — mapping only the common case misses where the effort really goes.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish routine, recurring exceptions worth mapping from one-off cases not worth mapping

contentSections.title: The path that's rare and the path that's expensive

contentSections.body: Larkspur's happy-path referral — insurer approves on first submission — takes about 15 minutes of Renata's time and resolves within a day or two. The exception path — insurer requests additional clinical documentation, which happens with two specific insurers roughly a third of the time — can take three weeks of back-and-forth, and Renata estimates it's most of what she actually spends her week on, even though it's a minority of total referrals.

Mapping only the happy path produces an accurate, useless map — accurate for the case that consumes the least effort, useless for the one that consumes the most. The instinct to map "the normal case" and treat exceptions as an appendix gets the effort allocation backward: if a third of cases eat most of a coordinator's week, that third *is* the process, in every sense that matters for deciding what to automate.

The complication is that not every exception deserves its own branch. A one-off — an insurer's website was down for a day, once, eighteen months ago — isn't worth mapping in detail; it's noise. A recurring exception — this specific insurer requests additional documentation on roughly a third of submissions, every month, predictably — is signal, and belongs in the map as a real, named branch, because it's going to keep happening at the same rate whether or not anyone draws it.

contentSections.scenario: While mapping Larkspur's referral exceptions, Renata mentions several things that happen "sometimes." You're deciding which deserve a real branch in the map and which are noise.
contentSections.question: Select every exception that's worth mapping as a real, named branch.

items.label: One specific insurer requests additional clinical documentation on roughly a third of submissions, every month
A second insurer routinely takes 10+ business days to respond at all, versus 2-3 for others
The office lost power for half a day once during a storm eight months ago, delaying everything that week
A referral was once faxed to the wrong number due to a typo, and nobody noticed for two weeks
The scheduling software double-books roughly one appointment per week due to a known sync bug with the calendar

explanation.insurer-docs: Worth mapping. A third of submissions, every month, from one specific insurer — this is a recurring, predictable pattern that will keep costing the same effort regardless of anyone's awareness of it. It belongs in the map as a real branch, not a footnote.
explanation.second-insurer: Worth mapping. A consistent, structural difference in one insurer's response time versus others is a recurring pattern with a known cause (that insurer's own processing speed), and it materially changes the timeline for every referral that goes to them.
explanation.power-outage: Not worth mapping as a branch. A single storm-related outage eight months ago is a one-off environmental event, not a recurring feature of the process — mapping it would clutter the map with something that isn't going to inform any automation or process decision.
explanation.wrong-fax: Not worth mapping as a recurring branch, though worth noting as a risk — a single typo-caused misfire is a one-off human error, not a pattern. If it happened routinely with a specific insurer or specific staff member, that would change the answer; as a single incident, it's noise for map purposes, though possibly worth a process safeguard regardless.
explanation.double-booking-glitch: Worth mapping. One per week, with a known, named cause (the calendar sync bug) — this is exactly the kind of recurring, systemic issue that belongs as a real branch, because it's predictable and will keep happening until someone addresses the underlying bug.

contentSections.synthesis: Three genuine recurring branches, two one-off noise events. The dividing line isn't how dramatic the exception sounds — a power outage sounds more dramatic than a documentation request, and matters far less to the map, because it isn't going to happen again next month in the same way. Recurring and predictable is what earns a place on the map; rare and unrepeatable doesn't, however memorable it was.

contentSections.title: How deep to map an exception
How far down the exception rabbit hole to go
contentSections.opening: You're mapping Larkspur's documentation-request exception branch with Renata. She starts describing sub-variations: sometimes the insurer wants a specific radiograph, sometimes a narrative justification letter, sometimes both, and the exact requirement seems to depend on which specific reviewer at the insurer picks up the case that day, which nobody at Larkspur can predict or control.

depth.situation: Renata is ready to keep going, listing every documentation-request variation she's ever seen, including some that happened once.
depth.question: How do you handle mapping this branch?

choices.label: Capture every variation Renata mentions, no matter how rare, to be thorough
choices.consequence: Two hours later you have a branch with nine sub-variations, three of which happened once each. The map is now harder to read than the process it describes, and nobody at Larkspur will be able to tell which sub-branches actually matter for planning.

choices.label: Map only the top-level branch (documentation requested vs. not) and skip the sub-variations entirely
choices.consequence: Faster, and it loses something real: the fact that the specific document required is unpredictable, insurer-reviewer-dependent, and therefore not something a rule-based system could reliably anticipate — which turns out to matter a great deal for what gets recommended later in this phase.

choices.label: Map the branch at the level of "documentation requested — type varies and is unpredictable per reviewer," naming the unpredictability itself as the mapped fact, without enumerating every historical variation
choices.consequence: This captures the thing that actually matters for later decisions — that this branch exists, is common, and is inherently variable — without drowning the map in one-off instances that won't recur in the same form.

over-mapped.summary: The map is now technically complete and practically unreadable. Nobody, including you, can look at it later and quickly answer "how often does this happen and what does it cost" — the signal is buried under every one-off variation Renata could remember.
over-mapped.lesson: Thoroughness that captures every instance instead of the pattern behind them isn't more accurate — it's noisier, and noise is its own kind of inaccuracy.

under-mapped.summary: The map is clean and readable, and it's missing a fact that turns out to matter: that the exception isn't just common, it's unpredictable in a specific way that changes what kind of fix would even work.
under-mapped.lesson: Simplifying a branch down to 'this happens sometimes' can lose the one detail — here, unpredictability itself — that determines whether the branch is automatable at all.

right-depth.summary: The map stays readable and captures the fact that actually matters: this branch is common, and its specific requirements vary unpredictably by insurer reviewer — a fact that will directly shape what kind of solution makes sense later, without the map drowning in one-off historical instances.
right-depth.lesson: Map the pattern, not every instance of it. The right level of detail names what's true and recurring about a branch — including 'this part is unpredictable,' when that's the honest fact — without enumerating every historical variation that produced it.

contentSections.body: Map the exceptions that recur, at the level of detail that captures what's actually true about them — including when the true thing is 'this varies unpredictably' — and leave the one-offs out. That's what separates a map worth building automation from than one that just looks thorough.

title: Practice — Turn Seven Messy Process Descriptions Into Maps

learningObjectives.text: Apply the shadow-process, trace, wait-time, correctable-map, and exception-mapping skills to new scenarios

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills. Untimed, and the set doesn't expire — do all seven now or spread them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Map a Process You Actually Know, End to End
description: Apply the whole module to a real process you have genuine access to — trace real instances, separate touch time from wait time, draw a correctable draft, and validate it with someone who actually does the work.

learningObjectives.text: Produce an accurate process map validated by someone who performs the work
Apply touch-time/wait-time analysis and exception-branch judgement to a real process

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick a process you have real, current access to — your own work, a volunteer role, a small business you're connected to, even a household process with more than one person involved. It needs to be real enough that you can trace actual instances and, ideally, check your map with someone who does the work, the same validation Larkspur's map needed.

contentSections.title: Map a real process end to end
contentSections.brief: Produce a process map of something real, built the way this module teaches: traced from actual instances, timed for touch versus wait, drafted to invite correction, and validated by someone who actually does the work — not designed from memory or assumption.
contentSections.deliverable: A process map with timings, handoffs and exception branches, validated by someone who does the work.

stages.title: Choose the process and find the shadow signals
stages.instructions: Pick a real process with at least one other person involved in running it. Before tracing anything, note any shadow-process signals you can already see — a spreadsheet, a habit, a workaround nobody wrote down anywhere official.
stages.checkpoint: You've named the process and at least one shadow-process signal, or explicitly noted that you looked and didn't find one.

stages.title: Trace two real instances end to end
stages.instructions: Trace two separate, real, recent instances of this process — either from your own memory of specific cases, or by asking someone who ran them. For each: list discrete steps, note elapsed time between them where you can estimate it, and flag any near-misses or dead-weight steps.
stages.checkpoint: You have two traced instances with discrete steps and rough timing, not a general description of 'how it usually goes.'

stages.title: Separate touch time from wait time
stages.instructions: For your traces, roughly estimate what share of the total elapsed time was active work versus waiting/queued. Identify the single largest wait, and name specifically who or what it was waiting on.
stages.checkpoint: You can state a rough touch-time percentage and name the largest wait and its cause.

stages.title: Draw a draft map and identify real exception branches
stages.instructions: Draw the map in a deliberately draft-looking form — sketch it, use bullet points, whatever signals "not finished" — using the process's own working vocabulary. Add branches only for exceptions you have real evidence recur (not things that happened once).
stages.checkpoint: The map is visibly draft, uses real working language, and any exception branches are backed by recurrence evidence, not a single memorable incident.

stages.title: Validate it with someone who does the work, and self-check
stages.instructions: If at all possible, show the draft to someone who actually performs this process and explicitly ask them to tell you everywhere it's wrong. If that's genuinely not possible for this process, note that limitation honestly rather than skipping validation silently. Then run the self-check below.
stages.checkpoint: The map has been shown to someone for correction, or you've stated plainly why that wasn't possible this time.

rubric.criterion: Built from real traced instances, not a general description
rubric.meets: Contains at least two specific, dated or identifiable instances with discrete steps, not a single abstracted 'how it usually works.'

rubric.criterion: Distinguishes touch time from wait time
rubric.meets: States a rough estimate of active-work share and names the largest identified wait and what it was waiting on.

rubric.criterion: Looks draft, not finished
rubric.meets: The visual presentation signals 'still correctable' rather than 'polished and authoritative.'

rubric.criterion: Uses the process's own working language
rubric.meets: Step labels reflect how the person doing the work actually refers to them, not generic or formal relabeling.

rubric.criterion: Exception branches are recurrence-backed
rubric.meets: Any branch beyond the happy path is justified by evidence it happens repeatedly, not a single remembered incident.

rubric.criterion: Validated, or the gap is honestly disclosed
rubric.meets: Either someone who does the work reviewed it and their corrections are reflected, or the map plainly states that validation wasn't possible and why.

contentSections.body: A map nobody who does the work has corrected is a hypothesis. Getting it corrected, even once, is what turns it into something you could actually recommend automating from.

title: Why nobody tells the consultant about the spreadsheet
description: The person who built the shadow-process spreadsheet you need to see has real reasons not to mention it — none of them are about hiding anything from you personally.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the common reasons staff don't volunteer information about workarounds
Recognise interview openings that make disclosure feel safe versus openings that shut it down

contentSections.title: The reasons nobody says it out loud

contentSections.body: You know Renata's spreadsheet exists — you spotted the browser tab in the walkthrough back in Mapping Work As It Is. In the formal kickoff interview, you ask an open question: "Walk me through how insurance verification works." Renata gives you the four-step official version, almost word for word from the handbook PDF. She doesn't mention the spreadsheet once.

This isn't Renata being evasive. There are several ordinary, non-suspicious reasons someone doesn't volunteer their own workaround, and they're worth knowing by name because each one calls for a different response:

**Fear of being automated away.** If "tell the consultant how you actually do it" sounds, even slightly, like "tell the consultant which parts of your job could be replaced," the safest answer is the official one.

**Embarrassment about the workaround itself.** A personal spreadsheet built because the official system doesn't hold enough information can feel like an admission that the official system — or her handling of it — is inadequate, rather than a reasonable adaptation.

**Assumed irrelevance.** She may genuinely believe you already know about it, or that it's too mundane to mention — "everyone just does that" is a common, honestly-meant reason for leaving something out.

**Assumed it's not your business.** A tool she built for herself, on her own initiative, can feel like personal property rather than process documentation, especially if nobody in management sanctioned it.

None of these require distrust of you specifically. All of them predict the same behaviour: the polished, official answer comes out first, and the real one only surfaces if something in the interview makes it safe to mention.

contentSections.scenario: Renata says, mid-interview, almost as an aside: "I mean, I have my own way of keeping track of which insurers are tricky, but that's probably not what you're asking about."
contentSections.question: What's actually happening in this moment?

options.label: She's testing whether you're paying attention
She's signalling, tentatively, that the shadow process exists — and waiting to see whether you treat it as relevant before saying more
She's being unhelpfully vague and should be asked to focus on the actual question

feedback.signal: Correct. "Probably not what you're asking about" is a hedge, not a dismissal — she's floated the topic and left the door open a crack, without committing to walking through it unless you signal it's welcome. This is the moment identified in the concept above: whether the real answer surfaces depends on what happens right here.
feedback.testing: There's no adversarial framing in this — nothing suggests Renata is trying to catch you out. Reading it that way risks responding defensively to an opening that was actually an invitation.
feedback.vague: Treating this as a lapse in focus and redirecting her back to the 'actual question' is exactly the response that closes the door she just opened — it confirms her hedge that this wasn't what you wanted to hear about.

contentSections.concept: People rarely announce a shadow process outright, especially to someone they've just met who's been hired to look at automating their work. They test the water with a hedge, and what happens in the next ten seconds determines whether the real information comes out. Treating the hedge as noise to redirect past is the single most common way an interviewer loses access to the most useful thing in the room.

contentSections.title: Making disclosure the easy option

contentSections.body: The fix isn't a trick question — it's removing the reasons above, out loud, before you need them not to matter. Naming explicitly, early, that workarounds are expected and valuable ("most places I work have at least one spreadsheet like this — it usually tells me more than the official process does") does real work: it reframes the disclosure from confession to contribution, and it tells Renata the automation conversation isn't secretly about her job security.

contentSections.scenario: You're opening an interview with a new team member at Larkspur's second location, hoping to surface any shadow processes early rather than stumbling onto them by accident later.
contentSections.question: Select every opening move that genuinely makes disclosure feel safe.

items.label: "Almost every team I've worked with has at least one workaround that isn't in any official document — what's yours?"
"To be clear, I'm here to understand the process, not to evaluate anyone's job performance or job security."
"I need you to tell me about any unofficial spreadsheets or shortcuts you use."
"If you've built something yourself to make this easier, that's exactly the kind of thing that tells me where the real process actually is."
"Management has asked me to find out exactly what everyone does day to day."

explanation.normalize: Genuinely helps. Naming that workarounds are the norm, not the exception, removes the 'admitting a personal failure' framing before it can even form.
explanation.not-about-jobs: Genuinely helps, directly addressing the fear-of-automation reason from this lesson — stating explicitly that this isn't a performance or job-security conversation removes the single biggest reason to withhold.
explanation.direct-demand: Doesn't help, and can backfire. Phrasing it as something you need from them frames disclosure as compliance rather than contribution, and 'unofficial' carries a faint whiff of rule-breaking that invites defensiveness.
explanation.credit-the-work: Genuinely helps. Framing a workaround as evidence of the person's own competence and initiative — which it usually is — is the opposite of the embarrassment reason from this lesson.
explanation.authority-frame: Doesn't help. Invoking management's request to "find out exactly what everyone does" sounds like surveillance, which activates every reason to withhold at once, especially the fear-of-automation one.

contentSections.synthesis: Three genuine openers and two that backfire. The pattern: the openers that work all reduce risk to the person being interviewed before asking for anything. The ones that fail all frame disclosure as something extracted for someone else's purposes.

contentSections.body: The official answer comes first because it's the safe one. Whether the real one follows depends on what you do in the first ten seconds after someone hedges — treat the hedge as an invitation, not a distraction.

title: Questions that get a story instead of a summary
description: "Does the process work well" gets you "yeah, it's fine." The rewrite that actually gets you something usable is more specific than it feels like it needs to be.

learningObjectives.text: Rewrite closed or summary-inviting questions into ones that elicit a specific story

contentSections.title: Why 'does it work well' gets you nothing

contentSections.body: "Does the referral process work well for you?" "Yeah, it's fine, mostly." That exchange takes eight seconds and tells you almost nothing — not because Renata is being unhelpful, but because "does it work well" is a summary question, and summarizing months of daily experience into a single adjective is exactly what any of us would do when asked that abruptly.

A summary question asks someone to compress a large amount of variable experience into one evaluative word — fine, okay, fine, fine. It's not that people are hiding the detail; the detail simply doesn't surface when the question shape doesn't ask for it. "Fine" is a true and honest and completely useless answer.

A story question asks for a specific, bounded episode instead: "Walk me through the last time it went wrong." This forces retrieval of an actual memory rather than a general impression, and actual memories come loaded with the detail a summary strips out — who was involved, what specifically went wrong, how long it took to notice, what they did about it. The shift is from asking someone to evaluate the process to asking them to narrate one instance of living inside it — which is, not coincidentally, the same shift covered in Mapping Work As It Is, applied here to what you ask rather than what you draw.

contentSections.code:
Interview script, question 4:
"So overall, would you say the prior-authorization process is working well, or are there issues?"
contentSections.question: What's wrong with this question, specifically?

options.label: It's too long
It's a summary/evaluation question dressed up as open-ended — it invites a general judgment ('working well' / 'there are issues') rather than a specific, retrievable memory
It should be asked earlier in the interview

feedback.summary-disguised: Correct. It has the grammatical shape of an open question — no yes/no answer forced — but functionally it's still asking for an overall evaluation, which produces the same compressed, low-detail answer as a closed question. 'There are issues, I guess' is exactly as useless as 'yeah, it's fine.'
feedback.too-long: Length isn't the problem — a longer question that anchors to a specific instance ("walk me through the last time this went sideways, from the moment you noticed something was off") would be more useful, not less, despite being longer.
feedback.wrong-order: Timing isn't the flaw here. The same question asked at any point in the interview would produce the same compressed, unhelpful answer, because the flaw is in what the question shape asks for, not when it's asked.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The tell is the word "overall." Any question that asks someone to evaluate across the whole sweep of their experience, rather than narrate one instance of it, will get you a compressed judgment instead of retrievable detail — no matter how the question is otherwise phrased or how open-ended it sounds.

contentSections.title: Rewriting on the fly

contentSections.problem: Rewrite the closed/summary question "Do the front desk and billing team communicate well about denied claims?" into a story question, and explain the specific change.

steps.label: Identify what's being asked to be evaluated
steps.work: "Communicate well" is an overall judgment about an ongoing relationship, not a specific event.
steps.why: Naming the abstraction is the first step — you can't fix a question until you see exactly what it's asking someone to summarize.

steps.label: Find the concrete event underneath the abstraction
steps.work: The underlying real event is: a claim gets denied, front desk finds out, billing needs to know, something happens (or doesn't) to communicate it.
steps.why: Every abstract evaluation is standing in for some class of specific, repeatable events. Finding that event is what gives you something to ask about directly.

steps.label: Write the story version
steps.work: "Walk me through the last time a claim got denied — how did the front desk find out, and what happened next in terms of who found out and when?"
steps.why: This asks for a specific, ordered sequence of events rather than a rating of a relationship, and it will surface exactly the kind of handoff-timing detail this phase's mapping module needs.

steps.label: Anticipate what this version will surface that the original wouldn't
steps.work: Likely to surface: who literally tells whom, how (email? in person? not at all until someone asks?), and how long that takes — none of which "do you communicate well" would have prompted.
steps.why: Predicting the kind of detail a rewrite should produce is a useful check on whether the rewrite actually fixes the original question, before you're relying on it live in an interview.

faded.problem: Second rewrite, same procedure. Original question: "Is the current appointment-reminder system effective?"

blanks.prompt: What's being asked to be evaluated? (a few words)
blanks.answer: the overall effectiveness of the reminder system
accept: how well the reminder system works overall
blanks.why: Naming the abstraction — 'effective' as an overall judgment — is what tells you this question needs the same rewrite treatment.

blanks.prompt: What's the concrete event underneath it? (one sentence)
blanks.answer: a reminder gets sent, a patient does or doesn't respond, and staff do or don't have to follow up
accept: a specific reminder being sent and whether the patient showed up or needed follow-up
blanks.why: The class of specific events "effectiveness" is standing in for is: reminder sent, patient response (or none), consequence.

blanks.prompt: Write the story version of the question.
blanks.answer: walk me through the last time a patient didn't respond to a reminder — what did you do, and did they show up anyway?
accept: tell me about the last patient who didn't confirm — what happened next
describe the most recent no-response case and what you did about it
blanks.why: This anchors to one real, retrievable case rather than asking for a summary judgment about the whole system.

blanks.prompt: What detail is this rewrite likely to surface that the original wouldn't?
blanks.answer: whether the follow-up call actually accomplishes anything, or whether patients show up regardless of the reminder system's outcome
accept: whether the follow-up actually changes the outcome
whether the reminder system does anything the patient wasn't already going to do
blanks.why: This is close to the finding this track's earlier lesson on tracing single items already surfaced — sometimes the honest answer a story question produces is 'this step doesn't actually change anything,' which a summary question would never get you to.

contentSections.procedure: **Name the abstraction being asked for → find the concrete, repeatable event underneath it → write a question anchored to one specific instance of that event → predict what detail it should surface.** Do this rewrite in your head, live, whenever an interview question you planned in advance comes out sounding like an evaluation instead of a story.

contentSections.body: If a question can be honestly answered in one word — fine, sometimes, mostly — it's a summary question. Rewrite it to ask for one specific, retrievable instance instead, and the detail you actually need shows up on its own.

title: Interviewing the person whose job you might automate
description: The billing coordinator whose task is being scoped for automation is a harder interview than any other stakeholder — not because she's uncooperative, but because the stakes for her are real and different from anyone else's in the room.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate the specific tactical and ethical demands of interviewing someone whose task is a candidate for automation

contentSections.title: The interview that's different

contentSections.body: You're back with Renata, three weeks into the engagement, and the conversation has turned specifically toward how much of her prior-auth submission process could be automated. She's answering, but her answers have gotten shorter, more careful, less like the detailed, opinionated person from the first interview. She's not being difficult. She's being rational.

Every other stakeholder interview in this phase is, roughly, low-stakes for the person answering — the practice owner isn't worried about being automated out of his own practice, and a patient recounting a scheduling headache has nothing personally on the line. Renata does. If the honest answer to "how much of this could be automated" is "most of it," she's being asked to describe her own obsolescence to the person who might recommend it.

That changes what a good interview here has to do. Three things matter specifically: **transparency about what's actually being scoped** — is this about her job, or about the submission step specifically, and can you honestly say which; **never promising an outcome you don't control** — you can be honest about what you're finding without promising her job is or isn't safe, because you often genuinely don't know yet, and a false promise costs more than an honest uncertainty; and **framing automation as removing the tedious 90% so she can do the judgment-heavy 10%**, when that's actually true — and being willing to say when it isn't, rather than defaulting to that reassuring frame regardless of the facts.

contentSections.title: Renata asks the question directly
contentSections.opening: Partway through the interview, Renata stops answering your question and asks her own: "Is this going to replace my job?"

asked.situation: She's looking at you directly, and the room has gone quiet in the way it does when someone's asked something real.
asked.question: What do you say?

choices.label: "No, of course not — this is just about making your job easier."
choices.consequence: It's comforting, and you don't actually know if it's true yet — you're three weeks into a diagnosis, not done with it. If the eventual recommendation does reduce headcount on this task, you've now been caught in a promise you made without grounds to make it, which costs far more trust than the discomfort of an honest answer would have.

choices.label: "I can't really speak to that, let's get back to the process questions."
choices.consequence: Technically honest, and it lands as a confirmation of her worst fear — refusing to engage with the question at all reads, to someone already anxious, as 'yes, and I don't want to tell you.' The rest of the interview gets noticeably shorter and more guarded.

choices.label: "I honestly don't know yet — I'm still mapping what actually takes your time. What I can tell you is I haven't seen anything yet that looks like it needs a person less than a computer for the judgment calls, only for the repetitive parts. I'll tell you straight once I actually know more, instead of guessing now."
choices.consequence: This is uncomfortable to say and it's true, on both counts — the genuine uncertainty and the genuine early signal about where the judgment work seems to sit. Renata visibly relaxes slightly, not because the uncertainty is gone, but because she now trusts you'll tell her the real answer when there is one. Later in the same interview, she volunteers, unprompted, a detail about how she decides which insurers to call versus email — something she hadn't mentioned in the first two interviews.

false-promise.summary: The reassurance felt good in the moment. If it later turns out to be untrue, Renata — and likely the rest of the team, since this kind of thing gets discussed — will remember that you said something you had no way to know was true, which damages every subsequent interview at Larkspur, not just this one.
false-promise.lesson: A comforting answer you can't actually stand behind costs more, eventually, than an honest uncertain one costs immediately.

confirmed-fear.summary: Refusing to engage with the question at all, even for defensible reasons, reads as confirmation to someone already bracing for bad news. The interview becomes noticeably less useful from this point forward, because Renata is now managing what she says rather than reporting what actually happens.
confirmed-fear.lesson: Silence in response to a direct, anxious question rarely reads as neutral — it reads as an answer, and usually the worst-case one.

trust-built.summary: Renata gets an honest answer instead of a comforting one, and the interview continues to yield real, unprompted detail — the direct payoff of trust built by not overpromising at the exact moment overpromising would have been easiest.
trust-built.lesson: A true 'I don't know yet, and I'll tell you when I do' outperforms a comforting guess — it's the same honesty this module opened with, applied to the hardest question an interview subject can ask.

contentSections.body: The interview that touches someone's own job security needs more honesty and less reassurance than any other interview in the engagement — a true 'I don't know yet, and I'll tell you when I do' outperforms a comforting guess every time.

title: Written and async interviews when calls aren't possible
description: A multi-site client with shift workers on different schedules can't all get on a call — building an async interview that produces comparably useful data takes real design, not just an emailed questionnaire.

learningObjectives.text: Design an async interview method that substitutes adequately for a live conversation
Identify which parts of a live interview genuinely can't be replicated async, and plan around the gap

contentSections.title: Five sites, three shifts, no shared calendar

contentSections.body: Larkspur's sixth location runs three overlapping shifts of front-desk staff, none of whom share more than an hour of overlap in a week, and the practice can't afford to pull anyone off the floor for a 45-minute call. You need their input on the referral process anyway. A generic emailed questionnaire is the obvious fallback, and it's usually a worse version of the interview, not an equivalent one — unless it's built deliberately.

A bad async substitute is a list of the same summary-shaped questions from the live version, sent as a form. It gets exactly the compressed, low-detail answers this module's second lesson already covered — "fine," "mostly," "no issues" — because writing a thoughtful, detailed answer to an open-ended prompt takes real effort, and most people won't spend that effort on a form that arrived in their inbox unprompted.

A good async interview is built differently: it asks for a specific artefact instead of a written narrative wherever possible — a screen recording of doing the task once, a photo of the sticky notes on their monitor, a forwarded example of an actual email exchange with an insurer. Artefacts carry detail a written summary strips out, the same way a traced instance beats a described process. Where a written answer is genuinely needed, the prompt should be as specific and story-shaped as a live question would be — "describe the last time this went wrong" translates to async fine; "tell us about your experience with the process" doesn't improve by being written down.

contentSections.intro: Assemble an async interview kit for Larkspur's third-shift front desk staff, who you'll never get on a live call. Three decisions.

fields.prompt: What should the core request be?

options.label: A written form with the same questions as the live interview script
A short screen recording of them actually doing the task once, narrating as they go
A phone call scheduled outside their shift, unpaid

feedback.screen-recording: Right. A recording of the actual task, narrated live, carries the detail a written summary would strip out — hesitations, workarounds, the exact sequence of clicks — while costing the staff member roughly the same time as doing the task normally, plus a few minutes of narration.
feedback.written-form: This inherits the summary-question problem directly — a form invites brief, compressed answers, and most people won't invest the effort in a detailed written narrative for something that arrived as an unprompted task.
feedback.off-shift-call: Technically live, and asking someone to give unpaid time outside their shift is a real cost to them for your convenience — it also risks resentment that colors the answers you do get, and it's avoidable given other options exist.

fields.prompt: If a written question is genuinely needed, what shape should it take?

options.label: "Describe your experience with the referral process."
"Tell us about the last referral that gave you trouble — what happened, and what did you do?"
"Rate the referral process from 1-10."

feedback.story-shaped: Right — the same story-versus-summary distinction from earlier in this module applies just as much in writing. A specific, bounded prompt gets a specific, bounded answer, whether spoken or typed.
feedback.generic: This produces the same compressed, low-effort answer a summary question always produces, and writing doesn't fix that — if anything it's worse in writing, since there's no interviewer present to follow up on a one-line answer.
feedback.rating: A number tells you nothing about what's actually happening — it's the written-form version of "does it work well," with all the same information stripped out and none of the detail a story would carry.

fields.prompt: How do you handle the fact that async has no live follow-up question?

options.label: Accept whatever comes back as final, since follow-up isn't possible async
Build in an explicit, low-effort way to ask one follow-up — a single reply, not a second full round
Require every answer to be exhaustively complete on the first pass to avoid needing follow-up at all

feedback.light-followup: Right. Async doesn't have to mean zero follow-up — a short reply asking about one specific thing that stood out in their recording or answer is low-cost for them and recovers most of what a live follow-up question would have gotten.
feedback.accept-final: This gives up real information for no reason — the whole value of a live interview's follow-up questions doesn't have to be sacrificed entirely just because the format is async; a light follow-up recovers most of it.
feedback.exhaustive-first: Asking someone to anticipate and answer every possible follow-up in their first response is an unreasonable burden that will either go unmet or produce an exhaustingly long submission nobody wanted to write — worse for everyone than a light follow-up loop.

contentSections.synthesis: Artefact-first, story-shaped prompts where writing is unavoidable, and a light follow-up loop instead of either zero follow-up or an impossible demand for completeness — this recovers most of what a live interview would surface, without asking anyone to give up unpaid time outside their shift.

contentSections.title: What still gets lost

contentSections.scenario: Even a well-built async interview kit doesn't recover everything a live conversation gives you. Before relying entirely on async data from the third shift, it's worth naming honestly what's still missing.
contentSections.question: Select every genuine limitation of even a well-designed async interview, compared to a live one.

items.label: You can't hear hesitation, sarcasm, or discomfort in someone's voice the way you can on a call
You can't notice something odd mid-answer and immediately ask 'wait, say more about that' before the moment passes
Async interviews always produce categorically less usable detail than live ones
It's harder to build the kind of rapport across an async exchange that makes someone comfortable volunteering something sensitive, the way Renata did after the honest answer in the case-sim
Async interviews take the client more staff-hours in total than a live call would

explanation.tone-nuance: A genuine, unrecoverable limitation. Vocal tone carries information — hesitation, discomfort, sarcasm — that a screen recording's narration only partially captures and a written answer captures not at all.
explanation.real-time-probe: A genuine limitation. The moment in a live interview where you notice something and ask about it immediately, while it's fresh, has no async equivalent — even a fast follow-up loop happens after a delay, by which point some of the immediacy and detail is gone.
explanation.less-detail-overall: Not accurate as a blanket claim — an artefact like a screen recording can carry more usable procedural detail than a rushed live interview would, because it captures the actual sequence of actions rather than someone's verbal description of it. The comparison depends on what kind of detail you need, not a fixed hierarchy.
explanation.rapport-building: A genuine limitation, and worth taking seriously given the previous lesson — an async exchange makes it harder to build the specific kind of trust that led Renata to volunteer something extra after an honest, uncomfortable answer. That kind of moment is much harder to construct without real-time presence.
explanation.scheduling-cost: Not necessarily true, and often the reverse — a well-built async kit can cost the staff member less total time than pulling them off shift for a live call, which is exactly why it was chosen for this scenario in the first place.

contentSections.synthesis: Three real, unrecoverable limitations and two overstatements. The honest position isn't 'async is just as good' or 'async is always worse' — it's naming specifically what's lost (tone, real-time follow-up, rapport-building for sensitive disclosures) so you know where to be more cautious about what an async answer might be missing, rather than treating it as interchangeable with a live one.

contentSections.body: A well-built async interview — artefact-first, story-shaped prompts, a light follow-up loop — recovers most of what a live one gets. It doesn't recover tone, real-time probing, or the trust built by an honest answer to a hard question in the moment. Know which you're missing before you rely on the data.

title: Separating what they said from what you concluded
description: "Front desk doesn't like verifying insurance manually" reads like a fact from an interview. It's actually your inference from body language, and writing it down as if Renata said it is how findings quietly become fiction.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish verbatim quotes, direct observations, and personal inferences in interview notes

contentSections.title: Three kinds of sentence in your notebook

contentSections.body: Your notes from the interview with the second location's front desk read: "Staff don't like doing manual verification." Read back a week later, this looks like a finding — a fact you can put in a report. Nobody actually said that sentence. What you saw was two staff members sighing when the topic came up and one of them saying "I mean, it is what it is." You wrote your interpretation down as if it were a quote.

Interview notes collapse three genuinely different kinds of information into one undifferentiated stream unless you actively keep them apart:

**Quotes** — the exact words someone said, ideally in quotation marks, ideally verbatim or as close as your note-taking speed allows.

**Observations** — what you directly witnessed that isn't speech: a sigh, a long pause, someone glancing at a colleague before answering, a screen showing 40 unread messages.

**Inferences** — your own conclusion about what a quote or observation means. "Staff don't like manual verification" is an inference drawn from a sigh and a resigned phrase — a reasonable one, maybe even correct, but categorically different from something anyone said or something you directly observed.

The danger isn't having inferences — you need them, that's the analytical work of this whole phase. The danger is writing them down indistinguishably from quotes and observations, so that a week later, or when someone else reads your notes, there's no way to tell which sentences are evidence and which are your interpretation of evidence.

contentSections.title: Where this actually bites you

contentSections.code:
Interview notes, front desk team, location 2:

"Staff resent the manual verification step and feel it's a waste of their skills. Renata mentioned insurers are difficult. The team is generally frustrated with the current system and wants change."
contentSections.question: Read purely as written notes — what's the core problem here?

options.label: The notes are too short

Every sentence is written as flat fact, with no way to tell which are direct quotes, which are observations, and which are the interviewer's own conclusions — the notes can't be checked against what actually happened
The notes should have included timestamps

feedback.unmarked-mix: Correct. "Resent the step and feel it's a waste of their skills" is a strong, specific interpretive claim written with the same flat confidence as "Renata mentioned insurers are difficult," which might be an actual paraphrase of something she said. A reader — including the notetaker, a month later — has no way to separate what was actually said or seen from what was concluded.
feedback.too-short: Length isn't the flaw. Even a much longer version of these same notes would have the identical problem if every sentence stayed unmarked as to its source — more words wouldn't fix the mixing of quote, observation, and inference.
feedback.no-timestamps: Timestamps would be a nice addition and aren't what's actually broken here. The core problem is that quotes, observations, and conclusions are indistinguishable from each other, which a timestamp does nothing to fix.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This matters beyond tidiness: a claim like "staff resent the step and feel it's a waste of their skills" is exactly the kind of finding that, if it ends up in a client-facing report, needs to be defensible — and "resent" and "waste of their skills" are strong words nobody in the notes actually said. If the client's operations director asks "who said that," the honest answer is nobody, that's an inference from a sigh — which is a very different thing to be caught saying you have evidence for.

contentSections.body: A finding that started as your inference and got written down as a quote is a fact you invented. Marking quotes, observations, and inferences separately as you write — not after — is what keeps your report defensible when someone asks 'who actually said that.'

learningObjectives.text: Apply the story-question rewrite and disclosure-safety skills from this module to new scenarios

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across this module's skills. Untimed, and the set doesn't expire.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Run and Write Up a Process Interview
description: Conduct a real interview about a real process, using this module's disclosure, story-question, and note-discipline skills, and produce a written record that keeps quotes, observations, and inferences properly separated.

learningObjectives.text: Conduct an interview using open, story-shaped questions that surface tacit process knowledge
Produce interview notes that separate quotes, observations, and inferences

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Interview someone about a real process they actually do — the same process you mapped in the previous module's lab, if that's available, or a different one with a willing subject. This lab produces the artefact that pairs with a process map: the record of what the person who actually does the work told you, and what you separately observed and concluded.

contentSections.title: Run and write up a real process interview
contentSections.brief: Conduct one real interview, 15-30 minutes, with someone who actually performs a process you're interested in. Use story-shaped questions, watch for hedges that signal a shadow process, and produce a written record that keeps what they said, what you observed, and what you concluded clearly separate.
contentSections.deliverable: An interview record separating quotes, observations and your own inferences.

stages.title: Prepare three story-shaped questions
stages.instructions: Draft three opening questions for your interview, each anchored to a specific, retrievable instance rather than a general evaluation — apply the rewrite procedure from lesson two if your first draft comes out summary-shaped.
stages.checkpoint: None of your three questions could be honestly answered in one word.

stages.title: Conduct the interview
stages.instructions: Run the interview. Open by naming, briefly, that workarounds and unofficial methods are exactly what you're hoping to hear about — the disclosure-safety framing from lesson one. Take notes live, and actively separate quote, observation, and inference as you write, rather than trying to sort it out afterward from memory.
stages.checkpoint: You have real notes from a real conversation, with at least one hedge or unprompted detail you followed up on rather than let pass.

stages.title: Write up the interview record
stages.instructions: Turn your live notes into a clean written record with three visibly separate categories: direct quotes, direct observations, and your own inferences (clearly labeled as such, not stated as fact). Include at least one specific instance the person walked you through in story form.
stages.checkpoint: A reader could point to any claim in your record and immediately tell whether it's a quote, an observation, or your interpretation.

stages.title: Self-check against the rubric
stages.instructions: Read your record as if you were the client's operations director, asking 'who actually said that' about your strongest claim. If you can't answer cleanly, fix the labeling before calling this done.
stages.checkpoint: Every claim in the record would survive being challenged with 'who said that, and how do you know.'

rubric.criterion: Questions are story-shaped, not summary-shaped
rubric.meets: Opening questions anchor to specific, retrievable instances rather than inviting an overall evaluation.

rubric.criterion: Disclosure safety is addressed explicitly
rubric.meets: The interview opens by naming that workarounds and unofficial methods are welcome and expected, not a confession.

rubric.criterion: Quotes, observations, and inferences are visibly separated
rubric.meets: A reader can immediately tell, for any given claim, which of the three categories it belongs to.

rubric.criterion: At least one specific traced instance is included
rubric.meets: The record contains a real, bounded episode the interviewee walked through, not only general statements.

rubric.criterion: Inferences are labeled as interpretation, not fact
rubric.meets: Every conclusion drawn from a quote or observation is explicitly marked as the interviewer's own reading.

rubric.criterion: Would survive a 'who said that' challenge
rubric.meets: Every claim in the record can be traced back to a specific quote or observation, or is honestly marked as unresolved.

contentSections.body: An interview record that survives 'who actually said that' is worth far more, later, than one that reads smoothly but can't be checked — the discipline of separating the three costs a little speed now and saves your credibility later.

She'd forgotten the spreadsheet existed

A short screen recording of the task, narrated
A 1-10 rating scale

It can't fully replicate real-time follow-up or the rapport built by an honest answer to a hard question in the moment

options.label: An observation is something you directly witnessed (a sigh, a pause); an inference is your own conclusion about what it means
An observation is always more reliable than a quote
There's no meaningful difference for note-taking purposes

It only matters if the client asks for the raw notes
