title: No baseline, no ROI — only a story
description: A claim that a change 'saved 10 hours a week' with no measurement of what the process cost before is a number nobody can check, including the person who said it.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an ROI claim without a pre-intervention baseline is unverifiable
Diagnose why a specific ROI claim can't actually be checked

contentSections.title: The number nobody can check

contentSections.body: Six months after Larkspur's fourth location switched practice-management software, the owner tells you proudly: "That new system has saved us at least ten hours a week on scheduling." You ask what scheduling took before the switch. He pauses. Nobody measured it. The ten hours is a feeling, dressed as a number.

This happens constantly, and it isn't dishonesty — it's the natural shape of hindsight. Once a new system is running and things feel smoother, it's easy to reach for a plausible-sounding number that fits the feeling. The problem isn't that ten hours is necessarily wrong. It's that nobody, including the person who said it, can actually check it, because the number it should be compared against — what scheduling cost before — was never recorded.

A baseline is the measurement taken *before* anything changes: how much time, how many errors, how much rework, at what volume, under the old process. Without it, any after-the-fact claim about improvement is a story that happens to use a number instead of an adjective. "It's a lot better now" and "it saved ten hours a week" carry the same actual evidence — none — dressed differently.

contentSections.scenario: The owner's "ten hours a week saved" claim is being repeated to prospective investors as a concrete ROI figure for the new system.
contentSections.question: What specifically makes this number unverifiable, rather than just optimistic?

options.label: Ten hours is probably too high an estimate
There's no pre-switch measurement to compare against — 'ten hours saved' requires knowing both the before and after time, and only the after exists
The owner isn't a reliable source of information about his own practice

feedback.no-comparison-point: Correct. 'Saved' is inherently a comparison — time-before minus time-after. With no recorded time-before, the claim has only one side of the subtraction, and no amount of confidence in the after-number fixes that; there's nothing to subtract it from.
feedback.too-high: This assumes the number is wrong in a specific direction, which isn't actually knowable either — it could just as easily be too low. The real problem isn't that ten hours is a bad guess, it's that there's no way to know if it's a good one.
feedback.unreliable-source: The owner isn't lying or being unreliable — he's reporting an honest, felt sense of improvement. The issue is structural, not about his credibility: a comparison claim needs two numbers, and only one exists.

contentSections.mechanism: Any claim shaped like 'X improved by N' is a subtraction — after minus before. If the before number was never measured, the claim can still be said with total sincerity, and it still can't be checked by anyone, including the person saying it. This is the single most common gap in ROI claims across automation projects generally, not just Larkspur's: the after-state gets measured because it's new and interesting, and the before-state was never worth measuring because, at the time, nobody was planning to compare anything.

contentSections.title: What this means for how you scope every engagement from here

contentSections.scenario: You're about to start a new engagement at Larkspur's fifth location, scoping automation for their supply-ordering process. Before any baseline work begins, you ask the office manager to guess: how many hours per week does she think the current manual ordering process takes across the team?
contentSections.question: She estimates 6 hours a week. Once you actually measure it over two weeks (this module's later lessons cover exactly how), what's a realistic range for how far off a confident, unmeasured guess like this typically is, as a percentage?
contentSections.explanation: Confident, unmeasured estimates of process time are commonly off by 30-50% in either direction — sometimes more — because people systematically under-count the small, frequent interruptions and over- or under-remember the rare bad days depending on how recently one happened. This isn't a knock on the office manager's honesty or attentiveness; it's simply what unmeasured recall does. It's also exactly why this module exists: a plausible-sounding number, however confidently stated, isn't a baseline until it's actually been measured.

contentSections.body: "Saved X hours" is a subtraction. If the before-number was never measured, the claim can't be checked — by you, by the client, or by anyone comparing it later — no matter how confidently it's stated.

title: Volume, time, error rate, rework: the four numbers
description: A baseline that's actually usable measures four specific things, defined precisely enough that the same measurement could be repeated by someone else and get roughly the same answer.

learningObjectives.text: Define volume, time, error rate, and rework precisely for a specific process

contentSections.title: Four numbers, precisely defined

contentSections.body: You're scoping the baseline for Larkspur's prior-authorization process, the one mapped and traced back in the earlier modules of this phase. "How's it going right now" isn't a baseline. Four specific numbers, each precisely defined, are.

**Volume** — how many requests move through the process in a given period. Not "a lot" — a count: Larkspur processes roughly 340 prior-authorization requests per week across six locations, based on two weeks of submission logs.

**Time** — both touch time (active work, from the mapping module) and total elapsed time (including queues). Larkspur's average touch time is about 12 minutes per request; total elapsed time, per the traced instances, runs from same-day to over a week depending on whether the request needs resubmission.

**Error rate** — how often the process fails on the first attempt and has to be redone. Roughly 18% of Larkspur's submissions get an initial rejection requiring resubmission, based on Renata's own spreadsheet tracking.

**Rework** — how many touches, on average, a request needs before it resolves. Larkspur averages 2.3 touches per request — most resolve in one, the 18% that get rejected typically need two or three more.

Each of these needs a stated definition, a stated source, and a stated period — "18% based on Renata's tracking spreadsheet, covering the last 6 weeks" is a number someone else could check or dispute. "It happens sometimes" isn't.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a precise definition for one of the four baseline metrics, for Larkspur's referral process specifically. Three decisions.

fields.prompt: Defining 'error rate' for prior-auth submissions — what should count as an error?

options.label: Any submission the insurer doesn't approve within 24 hours
Any submission rejected on first attempt and requiring resubmission with corrected information
Any submission Renata personally feels went badly

feedback.rejected-resubmit: Right. This is objective and checkable — a resubmission either happened or it didn't, and it's recorded in Renata's tracking. It captures the actual thing costing extra effort: having to redo the submission, not just how quickly the insurer got back.
feedback.slow-response: This conflates error rate with the insurer's own response speed, which is a separate, external factor covered more directly by the time metric — a slow-but-correct approval isn't an error in Larkspur's process, even though it's frustrating.
feedback.subjective-feel: Not checkable by anyone else, and not stable even for Renata herself day to day — a precise baseline metric needs a definition that produces the same answer regardless of who's counting or how they're feeling about it that day.

fields.prompt: What should be the recorded source for this number?

options.label: Renata's memory, asked directly in an interview
Renata's own tracking spreadsheet, read directly, over a stated period
The practice owner's general impression

feedback.spreadsheet-log: Right. A logged record, even an informal one like Renata's spreadsheet, is checkable and repeatable — someone could re-read the same six weeks of entries and get the same count. This is a genuine source of truth, distinct from anyone's memory of it.
feedback.memory: Memory is a reasonable starting estimate but isn't itself the baseline — per the predict-number exercise in the previous lesson, confident recall is commonly 30-50% off from a measured figure, which is exactly the gap a real baseline needs to close.
feedback.owner-impression: The owner isn't the person doing the work and has the least direct visibility into the actual rejection pattern — his impression is even further removed from the measured reality than Renata's own memory would be.

fields.prompt: How should the time period for this number be handled?

options.label: Leave it unstated — 'the error rate is 18%' is specific enough
State the exact period the number covers — e.g. '18%, based on the last 6 weeks of logged submissions'
Use 'typically' as a stand-in for a period

feedback.stated-period: Right. A rate without a stated period can't be checked or reproduced — six weeks in winter flu season might differ from six weeks in summer, and stating the window is what lets someone later ask a meaningful question like 'has this changed since then.'
feedback.unstated: An unstated period leaves the number's applicability ambiguous — 18% of what timeframe, measured when? This is exactly the kind of gap a skeptical reader will find first, which the last lesson of this module covers directly.
feedback.typically: 'Typically' sounds precise and specifies nothing — it's a word doing the work a real date range should be doing, and it can't be checked or reproduced by anyone else.

contentSections.synthesis: A checkable definition, a named source, and a stated period — together, these turn '18%' from a vibe into a number someone else could reproduce or dispute, which is the entire point of measuring a baseline in the first place.

contentSections.title: Computing rework from raw records

contentSections.problem: Renata's spreadsheet logs 40 prior-authorization requests from the last two weeks, with a column for how many times each was submitted before final resolution. Compute the average rework rate (average touches per request) from this raw data.

steps.label: Establish the raw counts
steps.work: Of the 40 requests: 33 resolved on the first submission (1 touch each). 5 needed exactly one resubmission (2 touches each). 2 needed two resubmissions (3 touches each).
steps.why: Rework has to be computed from the actual per-request counts, not estimated — this is exactly the kind of number a spreadsheet log makes possible that memory alone wouldn't produce reliably.

steps.label: Compute total touches across all 40 requests
steps.work: 33×1 = 33. 5×2 = 10. 2×3 = 6. Total = 33 + 10 + 6 = 49 touches across 40 requests.
steps.why: Summing total touches, not just counting how many requests needed rework, is what lets you compute a true average — a request needing three touches costs more than one needing two, and the average needs to reflect that.

steps.label: Divide to get the average
steps.work: 49 touches ÷ 40 requests = 1.225 average touches per request.
steps.why: This is the actual rework rate for this two-week sample — a single number that, if requests were representative of the broader pattern, could stand as a defensible baseline figure with its source and period stated.

steps.label: Note what this number does and doesn't tell you
steps.work: It tells you the average cost in touches per request. It doesn't, by itself, tell you which insurers or which staff drive the rework — that needs a further breakdown, not a reason to distrust the average.
steps.why: Naming a metric's limits honestly, rather than overselling what one summary number captures, is exactly the discipline this whole module is building toward — a baseline is a foundation, not the entire analysis.

faded.problem: Second computation, same procedure. A separate log of 25 customer support tickets shows: 18 resolved with one agent response, 5 needed two responses, 2 needed three responses.

blanks.prompt: What's the total number of responses across all 25 tickets?
blanks.why: Same method as the referral example — sum actual per-ticket counts rather than estimating an average directly.

blanks.prompt: What's the average rework rate (responses per ticket)?
blanks.why: Dividing total responses by total tickets gives the true average, the same computation as the referral example applied to a different dataset.

blanks.prompt: What does this 1.36 figure NOT tell you on its own, without further breakdown?
blanks.answer: which specific issues, agents, or ticket types are driving the rework
accept: which categories of ticket need more responses
blanks.why: The same honest-limits discipline applies here — a single average is useful and incomplete, and saying so plainly is part of presenting the number responsibly.

blanks.prompt: What would make this number defensible if presented in a report? (name the two things beyond the number itself)
blanks.answer: a stated source (the ticket log) and a stated period (the dates the 25 tickets cover)
accept: where the data came from and what dates it covers
blanks.why: The same pattern from the build-it exercise — a number is only as defensible as the source and period stated alongside it.

contentSections.procedure: **Get the raw per-item counts → sum the total → divide by the item count → state plainly what the resulting average does and doesn't tell you.** This same four-step computation works for rework rate, error rate, or any other averaged baseline metric.

contentSections.body: Volume, time, error rate, rework — each defined precisely enough that someone else could check it, sourced from a real record rather than memory, and scoped to a stated period. That's what makes a baseline a measurement instead of a guess with a decimal point.

title: Estimating when the data doesn't exist
description: Larkspur has no system logging which requests get rejected first-pass — Renata 'just remembers.' A defensible estimate is still possible without a clean database, if you're honest about the method.

learningObjectives.text: Apply low-cost estimation techniques (sampling, retrospective log review, structured recall) when clean data doesn't exist

contentSections.title: No BI system, no dashboard, no problem — mostly

contentSections.body: Larkspur's newest location has none of Renata's spreadsheet discipline. Nobody logs which submissions get rejected first-pass; the office manager "just remembers" that two specific insurers are difficult. You still need a baseline for this location. There's no database to query. There is still a defensible way to get a real number.

When clean logged data doesn't exist, three techniques, in rough order of preference, produce something better than a guess dressed as fact:

**Retrospective sampling** — pull whatever physical or digital trace does exist (fax confirmations, sent-folder emails, printed insurer responses) for a bounded, recent period, and manually count. Slower than reading a spreadsheet, faster than it sounds, and grounded in real records rather than memory.

**Time-boxed manual tally** — going forward, track a metric by hand for a short, defined window (two weeks is usually enough) before drawing conclusions, rather than trying to reconstruct the past.

**Structured recall with a stated confidence range** — when neither of the above is possible, ask the person directly, but frame it as a range with an honestly stated confidence, not a single confident number: "I'd guess 15-25%, and I'm not very sure" is more useful and more honest than "20%" stated flatly.

All three are estimates, and all three should be labeled as such in any report — the difference between them and a fabricated-sounding precise number is that they're honest about their own uncertainty and traceable to a real method.

contentSections.scenario: You're building a baseline for the new location's rejection rate with no existing log. Several approaches are on the table.
contentSections.question: Select every approach that's a genuinely defensible estimation technique, as opposed to an unreliable shortcut.

items.label: Manually counting rejection notices in the fax machine's saved confirmations for the last month
Having the office manager tally rejections by hand on a simple log for the next two weeks
Asking the office manager for a single confident percentage and reporting it as the rejection rate with no caveat
Asking the office manager for a range with a stated confidence level, and reporting it explicitly as an estimate
Using Renata's location's 18% rejection rate as a stand-in for this location, since they're both Larkspur
Looking up an industry-wide average dental prior-auth rejection rate and using that

explanation.fax-count: Defensible. This is retrospective sampling from a real record — slower than a database query, but grounded in actual documents rather than memory, and reproducible by someone else counting the same fax folder.
explanation.two-week-tally: Defensible. A short, defined, forward-looking measurement window produces real data, even without existing infrastructure — this is the time-boxed manual tally technique, and two weeks is usually enough to see a representative pattern.
explanation.confident-guess: Not defensible as presented. A single confident percentage with no caveat misrepresents the actual epistemic status of the number — it's memory, stated with a false precision that invites someone to treat it as measured fact.
explanation.ranged-recall: Defensible, specifically because it's honest about what it is — a range with a stated confidence level tells the reader exactly how much weight to put on it, which a flat single number doesn't.
explanation.borrow-other-location: Not defensible. Different locations can have meaningfully different insurer mixes, staff experience, and patient volume — borrowing another location's measured number and presenting it as if it applied here substitutes a real number from the wrong context for an honest estimate of the right one.
explanation.corporate-average: Not defensible for this purpose. An industry average smooths over exactly the location-specific, insurer-specific patterns a baseline needs to capture — it might be a useful sanity check, but reporting it as this location's baseline substitutes a different question's answer for this one.

contentSections.synthesis: Three genuine techniques and three shortcuts that look like data but aren't measuring the actual thing in front of you. The dividing line isn't how the number is obtained — it's whether the number reflects this specific process, in this specific place, honestly labeled for what it actually is.

contentSections.title: Running the sampling exercise

contentSections.question: You've decided to run a retrospective sample of the new location's fax-confirmation folder to estimate the rejection rate. Put these steps in the order that produces a defensible number.
steps: Define the exact period to sample (e.g. the last 4 complete weeks) before looking at any documents
Pull every fax confirmation from that period, not a convenience sample of whichever ones are easiest to find
Count total submissions and count how many show a rejection or request-for-more-information response
Compute the rate and note the sample size and period alongside it
State the estimate's limitations honestly — e.g. faxes lost or not filed wouldn't be captured
contentSections.explanation: Defining the period before looking at any documents prevents an unconscious bias toward picking a period that happens to look better or worse. Pulling every confirmation in that window, not a convenient subset, is what keeps the sample representative rather than accidentally skewed — grabbing 'whichever ones are on top of the pile' tends to overrepresent recent documents. Counting total submissions alongside rejections is necessary to compute a rate, not just a raw count of rejections. Stating the sample size and period alongside the number is what makes it checkable later. Naming the method's own limitation — faxes that were lost or never filed wouldn't show up at all — is the honest final step that keeps the estimate from being oversold as more complete than it actually is.

contentSections.body: No database doesn't mean no baseline — retrospective sampling from real records, a short forward-looking tally, or an honestly-ranged recall estimate are all defensible, as long as the method and its limits are stated plainly alongside the number.

title: The cost of an error, and who currently absorbs it
description: A denied prior-authorization isn't free to redo — it costs someone's time, sometimes a patient's appointment, sometimes a no-show. Naming exactly who pays that cost changes how a client hears the finding.

learningObjectives.text: Fully cost an error, including downstream and non-obvious costs
Identify which role or budget actually absorbs a given cost

contentSections.title: "We just resubmit — it's not a big deal"

contentSections.body: You raise the 18% first-pass rejection rate with Larkspur's practice owner. His response: "That's not really a cost — we just resubmit, no big deal." He's not being dismissive on purpose. From where he sits, nothing about a rejection shows up on any bill he sees. The cost is real and it's invisible to him specifically, which is a very different problem than the cost not existing.

A rejection that gets silently resubmitted still has a full cost — it's just distributed across people and consequences the owner's view of the business doesn't naturally surface:

**Direct labor cost** — Renata's time redoing the submission, which is real, measurable (roughly 15-20 extra minutes per rejection, per her own tracking), and comes out of time she'd otherwise spend on something else.

**Downstream patient cost** — the resubmission adds days to when the patient can be scheduled, which for some patients means a delayed procedure, and occasionally a no-show when the eventual appointment no longer fits their life.

**Who absorbs it** — none of this shows up as a line item anywhere. Renata absorbs it as unpaid-attention time she doesn't get back. The patient absorbs it as delay and inconvenience, sometimes as a missed or postponed procedure. Nobody's P&L shows "cost of first-pass rejections" as a number, which is exactly why the owner's instinct is that there isn't one.

contentSections.scenario: A rejected prior-auth for a routine filling gets resubmitted with the correct code the same day. The patient's appointment, originally scheduled for the following week, gets pushed back nine days while the resubmission clears. The patient, a parent juggling two jobs, has to reschedule childcare twice and eventually cancels the appointment entirely, saying she'll "deal with it later."
contentSections.question: Who bears the real cost of this specific rejection, and what is it?

options.label: Nobody — the resubmission itself was free, since it just took a few minutes of Renata's time

Renata absorbs the redo time, and the patient absorbs the delay, the childcare disruption, and ultimately a cancelled appointment — a cost that shows up nowhere on Larkspur's books but is entirely real
Only the insurer, since they're the one who rejected it

feedback.distributed-real-cost: Correct. This is what an undercounted error cost actually looks like traced through to its end: a few minutes of visible staff time, plus a genuinely lost appointment and a family's disrupted week, none of which appears in any financial report the owner would naturally see. The cost is real, specific, and currently invisible to whoever isn't directly experiencing it.
feedback.nobody: This is the exact assumption the owner started with, and the traced consequence shows it's wrong — 'no big deal' from the practice's accounting perspective doesn't mean nothing was actually lost. A cancelled appointment and a disrupted family are real costs, just not ones that appear on an invoice anywhere.
feedback.insurer-only: The insurer's rejection triggered this, but the insurer bears none of the downstream cost — they don't lose anything from Larkspur's resubmission or the patient's cancelled appointment. The cost lands entirely on Renata's time and the patient's actual life, not on the party who caused the rejection.

contentSections.concept: "Who absorbs the cost" is a separate question from "who caused the problem," and both are separate from "does it show up on a report anyone reads." A cost can be entirely real, specific, and traceable, and still be invisible to the person making budget decisions — because nothing about their normal view of the business surfaces it. Naming, specifically, who absorbs a given cost is what turns "that's not a big deal" into a conversation the owner can actually engage with, because now there's a real person and a real consequence attached to the number.

contentSections.title: Making the invisible cost visible without overstating it
Getting the owner to actually see the cost
contentSections.opening: You're presenting the rejection-rate finding to Larkspur's owner. He repeats his position: "We just resubmit, it's fine." You have the traced example of the cancelled filling appointment, plus Renata's own estimate that rejections cost her roughly 2-3 hours a week in redo time across all her locations combined.

present.situation: You're deciding how to make the real cost land without sounding like you're exaggerating a routine administrative hiccup.
present.question: How do you present this?

choices.label: Extrapolate the 2-3 hours a week into a large annual dollar figure using Renata's hourly rate, and lead with that number
choices.consequence: The extrapolated number sounds impressive and is built on a real weekly estimate stretched across a year with no allowance for holidays, slow weeks, or variance — the owner, who runs the numbers for a living, spots the overreach immediately and it undercuts the whole finding, including the parts that were solid.

choices.label: Lead with the specific traced example — the cancelled filling appointment — and pair it with Renata's own stated weekly time estimate, without extrapolating further than the data supports
choices.consequence: The specific story makes the abstract percentage concrete and human, and the weekly time figure stays exactly as solid as it actually is, without stretching it into a bigger number than the evidence supports. The owner goes quiet for a moment, then asks what it would take to fix it.

choices.label: Just repeat the 18% rejection rate figure again, more firmly
choices.consequence: The owner already heard 18% and already dismissed it as 'not a big deal' — repeating the same number, more firmly, doesn't give him any new reason to see it differently. Nothing changes.

overstated.summary: The extrapolated dollar figure gets picked apart, and the finding's credibility takes the hit along with it — even the parts of the analysis that were solid now read as suspect, because the owner has reason to wonder what else got stretched.
overstated.lesson: A real, specific, well-evidenced cost doesn't need to be inflated to land — inflating it risks the credibility of everything else in the report.

no-movement.summary: Repetition without a new angle doesn't change how the owner is hearing the finding — he already filed 18% under 'not a big deal' once, and hearing it again doesn't reopen that filing.
no-movement.lesson: A number that's already been dismissed usually needs a different kind of evidence to land the second time, not a louder version of the same one.

landed.summary: A specific, real story makes the abstract percentage concrete, and pairing it with an honestly-scoped time figure — not stretched into an inflated annual number — keeps the whole finding credible. The owner engages with the actual problem instead of dismissing or disputing the framing.
landed.lesson: Concrete, specific cost plus an honestly-scoped number outperforms either a bigger extrapolated figure or a repeated abstract percentage — because it makes the invisible cost real without overstating it.

contentSections.body: A cost that doesn't show up on anyone's report can still be entirely real — naming specifically who absorbs it, with one concrete traced example alongside the honestly-scoped number, is what makes it visible without overstating it.

title: Baselines that survive a sceptical finance team
description: A CFO's first question about any ROI case isn't whether the number is impressive — it's how you know it's true. A baseline built to answer that question survives; one that isn't gets thrown out along with the recommendation attached to it.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a baseline is defensible enough to survive skeptical scrutiny

contentSections.title: "How do you know these numbers?"

contentSections.body: Larkspur's owner brings your baseline findings to a meeting with his accountant, who's considering financing a practice-wide automation rollout. Her first question isn't about the recommendation. It's: "Who counted this, over what period, and how confident are you?" If the baseline doesn't already answer that question in writing, the meeting stalls right there.

A defensible baseline states, for every number in it, four things: the **method** (how it was measured — a logged count, a sample, a structured recall estimate), the **sample size or period** (how much data, over what window), the **confidence** (measured fact, or estimate with a stated range), and what's **assumption versus what's measured** (anything extrapolated or estimated is labeled as such, not blended in with the hard numbers).

This isn't about hedging everything into uselessness — a confident, precisely measured number should read as confident. It's about never letting a reader mistake an estimate for a measurement, or a measurement for something more precise than its actual sample size supports. A skeptical reader's job is finding the weakest claim in the document; a defensible baseline sheet has already found it first and labeled it honestly.

contentSections.code:
Larkspur Baseline Summary — Prior Authorization

Volume: 340/week
Touch time: 12 min/request
Error rate: 18%
Rework: 2.3 touches/request
Annual cost of rejections: $47,320
contentSections.question: The accountant rejects this document in the first two minutes. What's the single biggest reason?

options.label: The numbers are formatted as a list instead of a paragraph
Every number is stated with identical confidence and no visible source or period — a measured count and a computed annual dollar extrapolation sit side by side with nothing distinguishing them
The touch time figure should be in seconds, not minutes

feedback.no-provenance: Correct. Volume, touch time, error rate, and rework might all be solid, sourced numbers — but nothing on the page says so, or says where any of them came from or over what period. And the annual cost figure is a computed extrapolation sitting with exactly the same visual confidence as the measured figures above it, with no flag that it involved assumptions the reader hasn't seen.
feedback.formatting: Presentation style isn't the problem here — a clean list is perfectly readable. The issue is that readability was mistaken for defensibility; the numbers could be beautifully formatted and still fail the accountant's actual question, which is about their source and confidence, not their layout.
feedback.wrong-unit: Units are a minor, fixable detail and not what would cause a two-minute rejection — even if every unit were perfect, the document would still fail on provenance.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A skeptical reader's actual question, every time, is "how do you know this," and this document doesn't answer it anywhere — not for the measured numbers, which deserved to be shown as solid, and especially not for the $47,320 figure, which is presumably built from several of the numbers above it multiplied together and compounded with unstated assumptions about hourly cost and annual volume. A defensible version states the method and period next to each figure, and clearly separates the measured baseline from anything computed or extrapolated from it.

contentSections.title: Building the defensible version

contentSections.scenario: You're rewriting the Larkspur baseline summary to survive the accountant's scrutiny. You're deciding what to add to each figure.
contentSections.question: Select every element that genuinely makes a baseline number more defensible to a skeptical reader.

items.label: A short note on how each number was obtained (logged count, sample, structured recall estimate)
The exact date range or sample size each number covers
A clear label distinguishing measured figures from estimated ones
Reporting figures to more decimal places (e.g. 18.37% instead of 18%) to look more precise
Any computed or extrapolated figure (like an annual cost estimate) clearly separated from directly measured numbers, with its own assumptions stated
Using confident, unhedged language throughout regardless of how the number was actually obtained

explanation.method-note: Genuinely helps. Naming the method — logged count vs. sample vs. structured recall — is exactly what lets a skeptical reader calibrate how much weight to put on each figure.
explanation.period-stated: Genuinely helps. A rate or count without a stated window can't be checked or compared to a later measurement — this is the same discipline from earlier in this module, applied at presentation time.
explanation.confidence-label: Genuinely helps. Distinguishing measured from estimated prevents exactly the failure in the spot-flaw exercise — a reader mistaking an extrapolation for a hard number.
explanation.more-decimal-places: Doesn't help, and can actively hurt — extra decimal places on a number drawn from a two-week sample imply a precision the underlying data doesn't support, which a sharp reader will notice and hold against the whole document.
explanation.extrapolation-flagged: Genuinely helps, and directly fixes the spot-flaw document's biggest problem — separating a computed annual figure from the measured baseline it's built on, with its own stated assumptions, is what keeps the extrapolation from contaminating trust in the real numbers.
explanation.confident-language: Doesn't help when it papers over genuine uncertainty — language should match the actual confidence of each number; using uniformly confident phrasing for both a solid logged count and a rough structured-recall estimate misrepresents the second one.

contentSections.synthesis: Four genuine improvements, two that actively backfire. The pattern in the two failures: both try to make the document look more authoritative — through false precision or uniformly confident language — rather than actually being more defensible, and a reader whose job is skepticism tends to notice the difference.

contentSections.body: A defensible baseline states its method, its period, and what's measured versus estimated, next to every number — not to hedge, but because that's the exact information a skeptical reader needs before they'll trust anything built on top of it.
