learningObjectives.text: Apply baseline-definition, estimation, cost-attribution, and defensibility skills from this module to new scenarios

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills. Untimed, and the set doesn't expire.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Baseline a Real Process With the Data Actually Available
description: Apply this module's four metrics, estimation techniques, and defensibility standards to a real process, using whatever data actually exists — not the data you wish existed.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a defensible baseline sheet using volume, time, error rate, and rework, with sources and confidence stated
Apply appropriate estimation techniques where clean data doesn't exist

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Use the same real process from the earlier modules in this phase if you have it, or a different real process you have genuine access to. This lab produces the number-side companion to the process map and interview record: an actual, defensible baseline, built honestly from whatever data really exists.

contentSections.title: Baseline a real process, honestly
contentSections.brief: Build a baseline sheet for a real process using this module's four metrics — volume, time, error rate, rework — sourced from whatever real data you actually have access to, using estimation techniques where clean logs don't exist, and stating method, period, and confidence for every figure.
contentSections.deliverable: A baseline sheet with sources, assumptions and confidence stated per number.

stages.title: Assess what data actually exists
stages.instructions: For your chosen process, check what real records exist for each of the four metrics — logged data, informal records (a spreadsheet, an inbox), or nothing. Be honest about the gaps rather than assuming you'll figure it out later.
stages.checkpoint: You have a clear map of which of the four metrics have real data available and which don't.

stages.title: Measure or sample what has real data
stages.instructions: For any metric with a usable real record, do the actual counting or sampling — don't estimate what you could measure. State the period or sample size explicitly as you go.
stages.checkpoint: At least one metric is backed by an actual count from a real record, with its period or sample size noted.

stages.title: Estimate what doesn't have clean data
stages.instructions: For any metric with no usable record, apply one of this module's estimation techniques — a short forward tally if you have time to wait for it, or a structured recall estimate with an honest range and confidence level if you don't.
stages.checkpoint: Every metric in your baseline is either measured or explicitly labeled as an estimate, with its technique named.

stages.title: Name who absorbs the cost of the process's main error or rework pattern
stages.instructions: For whatever your error-rate or rework figure represents, write one or two sentences naming specifically who absorbs that cost and how — following the pattern from lesson four, not just noting that a cost exists in the abstract.
stages.checkpoint: You've named a specific person, role, or party who bears the cost, not just a general statement that rework 'has a cost.'

stages.title: Write the defensible baseline sheet and self-check
stages.instructions: Assemble the four metrics into a clean sheet, with method, period/sample size, and confidence (measured vs. estimated) stated next to each one. Then run the self-check below, imagining a skeptical reader asking 'how do you know this' about your weakest figure.
stages.checkpoint: Every number in the sheet states its method, period, and confidence — nothing sits unlabeled.

rubric.criterion: Covers all four metrics: volume, time, error rate, rework
rubric.meets: Each metric is present, precisely defined for this specific process, and clearly stated.

rubric.criterion: Method and source are stated for every number
rubric.meets: A reader can tell, for each figure, whether it's a logged count, a sample, or an estimate, and where it came from.

rubric.criterion: Period or sample size is stated for every number
rubric.meets: No figure is presented without a window or sample size it applies to.

rubric.criterion: Estimates are honestly distinguished from measurements
rubric.meets: Anything not directly measured is clearly labeled as an estimate, ideally with a stated confidence range.

rubric.criterion: Cost attribution names who actually absorbs it
rubric.meets: At least one specific person, role, or party is named as bearing the cost of the process's main error or rework pattern.

rubric.criterion: Would survive a skeptical 'how do you know this' challenge
rubric.meets: No figure implies more precision or certainty than its actual method supports.

contentSections.body: A baseline built honestly from whatever data actually exists, with its method and confidence stated plainly, is worth more to a client than a more impressive-looking number nobody can check.

title: Checkpoint — Measuring Before You Change Anything
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous one, two from earlier in this phase. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Measuring Before You Change Anything

questions.from: This module — Measuring Before You Change Anything
questions.prompt: Why is 'saved 10 hours a week' unverifiable without a pre-intervention baseline?

options.label: It's inherently a subtraction, before-time minus after-time, and without a recorded before-number there's nothing to subtract from
10 hours is always an unrealistic figure
The person making the claim is being dishonest

questions.explanation: Any 'X improved by N' claim requires both sides of a comparison. Larkspur's owner wasn't lying — the claim is structurally unverifiable because only the after-state was ever observed.

questions.from: This module — Measuring Before You Change Anything
questions.prompt: What are the four baseline metrics this module defines?

options.label: Volume, time, error rate, rework
Cost, speed, quality, satisfaction
Revenue, headcount, turnover, margin

questions.explanation: Volume (how much moves through), time (touch and elapsed), error rate (first-attempt failure), and rework (average touches to resolution) — each defined precisely enough to be checked.

questions.from: This module — Measuring Before You Change Anything
questions.prompt: When no clean logged data exists, which estimation technique does this module rank as strongest?

options.label: A single confident guess from the most experienced staff member
Retrospective sampling from whatever real records do exist (fax confirmations, sent folders), followed by a forward tally, followed by structured recall with a stated range
Borrowing a comparable site's measured number

questions.explanation: Retrospective sampling from real records is preferred when possible; a time-boxed forward tally is next; a structured, honestly-ranged recall estimate is the fallback when neither is possible.

questions.from: This module — Measuring Before You Change Anything
questions.prompt: Why did Larkspur's owner initially believe rejections weren't 'a big deal'?

options.label: The cost genuinely doesn't exist
The cost is real but distributed across Renata's redo time and patients' delayed appointments — none of which shows up on any report the owner naturally sees
He was being deliberately dismissive

questions.explanation: A cost can be entirely real and specific while being invisible to whoever isn't directly experiencing it, because nothing about their normal view of the business surfaces it.

questions.from: This module — Measuring Before You Change Anything
questions.prompt: In the case-sim about presenting the rejection-rate cost, why did extrapolating to a large annual dollar figure backfire?

options.label: The owner didn't understand the math
The extrapolation stretched a real weekly estimate further than the evidence supported, and being caught overstating one number undercut trust in the whole finding
Annual figures are never appropriate in a business case

questions.explanation: A real, specific, well-evidenced cost doesn't need inflating to land — inflating it risks the credibility of everything else in the report, including the solid parts.

questions.from: This module — Measuring Before You Change Anything
questions.prompt: What four things does a defensible baseline number need stated alongside it?

options.label: Method, period/sample size, confidence level, and whether it's measured or estimated
A chart, a comparison to industry average, a forecast, and a recommendation
More decimal places to look precise

questions.explanation: These four elements are what let a skeptical reader calibrate exactly how much weight to put on a number, rather than mistaking an estimate for a measurement or vice versa.

questions.from: This module — Measuring Before You Change Anything
questions.prompt: Why does adding more decimal places to a baseline figure (e.g. 18.37% instead of 18%) tend to hurt its credibility?

options.label: It implies more precision than a small, informal sample actually supports
Decimal places are always wrong in business reports
It makes the document harder to read

questions.explanation: False precision — implying a level of measurement rigor the underlying data doesn't have — tends to be noticed by a sharp reader and undermines trust rather than building it.

questions.from: Previous module — Getting the Truth Out of People
questions.prompt: Why is 'walk me through what happened to this exact request' better than 'how does the process work'?

options.label: It anchors the answer to a specific memory instead of inviting a polished, idealized summary
It's a shorter question
It avoids technical language

questions.explanation: Baseline data collection often depends on getting real, specific instances from people, not summarized impressions — the same story-versus-summary principle from interviewing applies directly to gathering baseline evidence.

questions.from: Previous module — Getting the Truth Out of People
questions.prompt: What's the difference between an observation and an inference in interview or field notes?

options.label: An observation is something directly witnessed; an inference is your own conclusion about what it means
An observation is always more reliable than a quote
There's no meaningful difference

questions.explanation: This same discipline matters in baseline work — a note like 'staff feel rejections are a big deal' needs to be traceable back to something actually said or measured, not stated as flat fact.

questions.from: Earlier in this phase — Mapping Work As It Is
questions.prompt: What's the difference between the documented process and the shadow process?

options.label: The documented process describes intent; the shadow process is what actually keeps the work running
The shadow process is always a sign of noncompliance
They're always identical in a well-run organisation

questions.explanation: Renata's spreadsheet — the shadow process from earlier in this phase — turned out to be exactly the kind of real record this module's estimation lesson teaches you to sample from when no formal log exists.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: The bottleneck is rarely where the complaints are
description: Everyone at Larkspur complains about the fax machine. Once the process is actually mapped and baselined, the real bottleneck is a three-day wait in one specific insurer's callback queue — something nobody had mentioned unprompted.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish loud, visible friction from the process's actual time and cost bottleneck using mapped and baselined data

contentSections.title: Loud and expensive are different axes

contentSections.body: Ask anyone at Larkspur what's wrong with the referral process and the answer is immediate and unanimous: the fax machine. It jams, it's slow, everyone hates it. Now look at the traced timelines and the baseline from the last two modules of this phase: the fax step itself takes under two minutes per referral. The actual three-day wait in the process is a specific insurer's callback queue — a step nobody mentioned unprompted, because waiting isn't something anyone does *to* the fax machine, it just happens, quietly, to everyone.

Complaints cluster around whatever is annoying to interact with — a jammed machine, a clunky login screen, a confusing form. Cost and time cluster around whatever's actually slow or error-prone, which is very often something nobody actively interacts with at all: a queue, a wait, an external dependency. These are different axes, and the mistake is assuming they're the same one because complaint volume feels like it should correlate with actual cost.

This isn't a claim that complaints are worthless — a universally hated step is real data about something. It's a claim that complaint volume measures visibility and annoyance, not necessarily where the time and money actually go, and by this point in the engagement you have the traced timelines and baseline numbers from the previous two modules specifically so you don't have to guess which is which.

contentSections.scenario: Larkspur's front desk unanimously names the fax machine as the referral process's biggest problem. The traced timelines from earlier in this phase show: fax transmission takes under 2 minutes; the callback queue for one specific insurer (referred to internally as 'the slow one') averages 3 business days before anyone there even looks at a submission.
contentSections.question: Why does everyone complain about the fax machine and nobody mentions the callback queue, given that the queue is by far the bigger cost?

options.label: The fax machine is actually the bigger problem and the traced data is wrong

The fax machine produces an active, annoying, interactive failure (a jam, a delay someone has to notice and deal with) while the callback queue is a passive wait nobody actively experiences — it just silently elapses in the background
Staff don't know the callback queue exists

feedback.active-vs-passive: Correct. A jammed fax machine demands someone's attention right now — it's an active, interruptive failure. A three-day wait for a callback doesn't interrupt anyone; a request goes in, and time passes, and nobody's actively doing anything different during those three days. Active, interruptive friction gets complained about. Passive waiting, however costly, usually doesn't.
feedback.data-wrong: There's no reason to doubt the traced data here — two minutes of transmission time versus three days of queue time is a large, unambiguous gap, and it's consistent with the touch-time-versus-wait-time pattern already established in the mapping module of this phase.
feedback.unaware: Staff are generally aware the slow insurer exists — Renata's own tracking spreadsheet, from earlier in this phase, specifically flags this insurer. Awareness isn't the gap; it's that a known, accepted wait doesn't generate the same ongoing complaint energy as an active daily annoyance.

contentSections.mechanism: This is the same touch-time-versus-wait-time distinction from process mapping, applied to what people choose to complain about rather than what they measure. An active friction point gets noticed every single time it happens, because it demands a reaction. A passive wait, however large, blends into the background because nobody is doing anything differently while it elapses — which is exactly why it doesn't show up in an unprompted list of complaints, and exactly why the baseline data, not the complaint list, has to be the actual source for identifying the bottleneck.

contentSections.title: Using what you already measured

contentSections.scenario: Given the traced and baselined data from this phase: fax transmission takes under 2 minutes; the slow insurer's callback queue averages 3 business days; Renata's rejection-and-resubmission cycle (from the measuring module) adds an average of 2.3 touches per request when it happens, at an 18% rate.
contentSections.question: If Larkspur's owner insists on fixing the fax machine first because it's the most-complained-about step, roughly what share of a typical delayed referral's total elapsed time would that fix actually address?
contentSections.explanation: Two minutes of fax transmission time is a rounding error against a process where the callback queue alone can run 3 business days (well over 1,000 minutes of business time) and the rejection cycle, when it triggers, adds days more. Fixing the fax machine would address well under 5% of the actual delay in a typical held-up referral — it would make an annoying step less annoying, without meaningfully changing how long referrals actually take. This is exactly why the complaint list and the baseline data need to be treated as two different inputs, not one.

contentSections.body: What people complain about tells you what's annoying to interact with. What the traced and baselined data show tells you where the time and cost actually go. Use the second one to find the bottleneck — the first one is real, but it's answering a different question.

title: Frequency times pain: ranking candidates honestly
description: Once you have several real automation candidates, ranking them by gut feeling reproduces whatever bias is already in the room — a simple, honest formula does better.

learningObjectives.text: Rank automation candidates using frequency, pain, and feasibility rather than intuition or the loudest complaint

contentSections.title: The formula, and what it corrects for

contentSections.body: You now have five real candidates for automation at Larkspur, drawn from the mapping, interviewing, and measuring work across this phase: the slow-insurer callback queue, the referral-note-to-spreadsheet handoff, the appointment-reminder confirmation calls, the rejected-submission resubmission cycle, and the vendor-name inconsistency across locations' invoicing (a smaller side-finding from the process work). Ranking these by which one the owner mentioned first, or which one you personally find most interesting to solve, will produce a worse list than a simple, explicit formula.

**Frequency × pain**, with feasibility as a filter rather than a factor in the initial score, is the formula: how often does this happen (from your volume baseline), multiplied by how much it costs when it does (time, money, or human cost per occurrence, from your baseline and cost-attribution work) — producing a rough total-impact score you can actually compare across candidates, rather than five separate gut feelings about five different problems.

Feasibility — how hard this would actually be to fix, and with what — comes in as a second pass, not baked into the first score, because conflating "how much this matters" with "how easy this would be" tends to quietly bias the ranking toward whatever's easiest rather than whatever's most worth doing. Rank by impact first. Then look at feasibility to decide what's worth tackling given real constraints — the two lists together, not blended into one.

contentSections.scenario: You're scoring the five Larkspur candidates. Someone on the team suggests a few shortcuts to speed up the ranking.
contentSections.question: Select every approach that's a genuine, defensible way to rank these candidates by actual impact.

items.label: Score each candidate as (how often it happens) × (cost per occurrence), using the baseline data already gathered
Rank by whichever one the practice owner mentioned first in conversation
Rank by which one looks easiest to fix, since quick wins build momentum
Score impact first using frequency and pain, then apply feasibility as a separate, second-pass filter
Rank by whichever problem came up most recently in conversation
Estimate the actual per-occurrence cost (time, money, or downstream harm) for each candidate using earlier baseline and cost-attribution work

explanation.freq-times-pain: Defensible. This uses the actual measured data from earlier in the phase, and produces a comparable score across candidates instead of five disconnected impressions.
explanation.owner-priority: Not defensible as a ranking method — what the owner happens to mention first reflects recency, personal irritation, or whatever's top of mind, not a measured comparison of actual impact across candidates.
explanation.easiest-first: Not defensible as the primary ranking criterion — this bakes feasibility into the same score as impact, which systematically biases toward whatever's easiest rather than whatever matters most. Feasibility belongs as a separate, later filter, not the first sort.
explanation.separate-feasibility-pass: Defensible. Keeping impact and feasibility as two distinct passes, rather than blending them into one score, is what keeps the ranking honest about what actually matters most before constraints get applied.
explanation.most-recent-complaint: Not defensible. Recency is a property of conversation timing, not of actual cost or frequency — this is the same trap as owner-priority, just triggered by a different accident of timing.
explanation.cost-per-occurrence: Defensible. This is the 'pain' half of the formula, grounded in the actual cost-attribution work from the measuring module — who absorbs the cost, and how much, per occurrence.

contentSections.synthesis: Two genuine components of a defensible ranking, and three shortcuts that all substitute some accident of the conversation — who mentioned it, when, how easy it looks — for an actual measurement of impact. The formula isn't more work than the shortcuts; it just uses data you already have instead of whichever impression happens to be loudest in the room.

contentSections.title: Scoring two candidates, then two more

contentSections.problem: Score two of the five Larkspur candidates using frequency × pain, with real numbers from earlier baseline work: (1) the slow-insurer callback queue — happens on roughly 60 of the 340 weekly requests (the share that go to that specific insurer), costs roughly 3 business days of delay per occurrence; (2) the appointment-reminder confirmation calls — happens on nearly all appointments, costs about 4 minutes of staff time per call when a follow-up call is needed, which is roughly 30% of appointments.

steps.label: Establish a comparable unit for 'pain' across both candidates
steps.work: Convert both into a rough weekly cost. Callback queue: 60 occurrences/week × 3 days delay each = a large, cumulative scheduling-disruption cost, though not a direct staff-minutes figure. Reminder calls: roughly 30% of, say, 200 weekly appointments = 60 calls/week × 4 minutes = 240 staff-minutes/week.
steps.why: Frequency and pain need a shared unit to actually compare candidates against each other — 'days of delay' and 'minutes of staff time' aren't directly comparable without translating at least one of them into a common frame, like weekly cost.

steps.label: Note where the comparison is genuinely apples-to-oranges
steps.work: The callback queue's cost is mostly patient-experienced delay, not staff time — closer to what the previous module's cost-attribution lesson called downstream cost. The reminder-call cost is almost entirely direct staff labor time.
steps.why: Forcing everything into a single number can hide that these are different kinds of cost, one falling on staff hours and one falling on patient experience — both real, but worth naming separately rather than pretending a single blended score captures everything that matters.

steps.label: State the honest ranking, with the caveat
steps.work: By pure frequency, the reminder-call rework is more common (60/week) but each occurrence costs far less (4 minutes) than the callback-queue delay (3 days each), even though the queue affects fewer requests overall. Total impact likely favors the callback queue as higher priority, but the reminder-call fix might be far easier to implement — which is exactly the separate feasibility pass to run next, not a reason to blend it into this score.
steps.why: The honest output of a ranking exercise is sometimes 'these aren't directly comparable on one axis, here's the reasoning' rather than a single clean number — presenting false precision here would repeat the mistake from the baseline-defensibility lesson.

steps.label: Flag what's still needed before recommending anything
steps.work: A feasibility pass on both: how hard would fixing the callback queue actually be, given it depends on an external insurer's own process? How hard would automating reminder-call triage be, given it's entirely within Larkspur's own systems?
steps.why: This sets up exactly the analysis this module's later lessons need — impact ranking alone isn't a recommendation yet.

faded.problem: Score the remaining two candidates the same way: (3) referral-note-to-spreadsheet handoff — happens on all referrals (say 80/week across the practice), costs a variable 1-4 day delay depending on how quickly the office manager notices, averaging roughly 1.5 days; (4) vendor-name inconsistency in invoicing — happens on maybe 15 invoices/week, costs about 10 minutes of manual reconciliation each when it occurs.

blanks.prompt: What's the rough weekly cost for the referral handoff, in the same 'delay' unit as the callback queue example?
blanks.answer: 80 occurrences/week × ~1.5 days average delay each = a large cumulative scheduling-disruption cost, similar in kind to the callback queue
accept: 80 referrals a week at about 1.5 days delay each, a large cumulative delay
roughly 120 referral-days of delay per week
blanks.why: Same method as the callback queue — occurrences times per-occurrence cost, in the same unit (days of delay) so it's comparable to that candidate specifically.

blanks.prompt: What's the rough weekly cost for the vendor-name inconsistency, in staff-minutes?
blanks.why: Same method as the reminder calls — occurrences times per-occurrence staff time, giving a comparable weekly staff-minutes figure.

blanks.prompt: Which of these four candidates now looks like the highest-impact, based on frequency × pain alone?
blanks.answer: the referral-note-to-spreadsheet handoff, since it affects all 80 weekly referrals at a substantial average delay, making its cumulative delay cost likely the largest of the four
accept: the referral handoff, because it's both frequent and high-delay
referral handoff — highest combination of frequency and per-occurrence cost
blanks.why: This surfaces a genuinely important finding purely from the arithmetic: the handoff delay affects every referral, not just the ones going to one slow insurer, which makes its total cumulative impact larger even though no individual occurrence is as dramatic as the 3-day callback wait.

blanks.prompt: What's the one thing this ranking still can't tell you, that the next step needs to answer?
blanks.answer: how feasible each fix actually is — the referral handoff might be a simple internal process fix while the callback queue depends on an external insurer Larkspur doesn't control
accept: feasibility — how hard each one would actually be to fix
whether Larkspur can actually control or change each bottleneck
blanks.why: Impact ranking and feasibility are deliberately kept as two separate passes — the highest-impact item isn't automatically the right one to tackle first if it's also the hardest to actually change.

contentSections.procedure: **Convert frequency and pain into a comparable unit → note where the comparison is genuinely apples-to-oranges rather than forcing false precision → state the honest ranking with caveats → run feasibility as a separate second pass.** This produces a defensible priority order instead of a gut-feeling list.

contentSections.body: Frequency times pain, using the baseline data you already gathered, produces a comparable, defensible ranking — feasibility comes after, as its own pass, so the easiest fix doesn't quietly displace the one that actually matters most.

title: The step everyone hates that costs almost nothing
description: Staff universally hate re-typing insurer names into two separate systems. It takes 90 seconds and never causes an actual error — automating it would be popular and nearly worthless.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a universally disliked step from a genuinely costly one, and recognise when they diverge

contentSections.title: Hated and expensive are not the same axis either

contentSections.body: Every single person interviewed at Larkspur, unprompted, mentioned having to re-type an insurer's name into both the scheduling software and the billing software — the two don't sync. It's universally disliked. It's also, per the baseline data, a 90-second task that never once shows up in Renata's rejection log as a cause of an actual error, because both systems auto-suggest from a dropdown and typos get caught before submission.

This is a different trap than the fax machine from lesson one — this time the step *is* getting complained about loudly and unanimously, which makes it feel like the obvious automation target. But 'universally hated' and 'expensive to keep doing manually' are still two different measurements, and this step scores high on the first and low on the second.

A step can be hated because it's tedious and repetitive without being costly, if it's fast and reliably error-free. Automating it would make everyone happier day to day — that's real and not nothing — but it wouldn't move the frequency × pain score from the previous lesson, because the actual cost per occurrence is small. The honest framing for a finding like this: worth doing eventually for morale and goodwill, not worth prioritizing as a high-impact automation investment, and it's important to say both halves of that sentence rather than letting 'automate this too' get bundled quietly into the same recommendation as the callback queue.

contentSections.scenario: You're sorting Larkspur's known friction points into genuine automation priorities versus low-cost annoyances, using both the complaint list and the baseline data.
contentSections.question: Select every step that's a genuine high-priority automation candidate, as opposed to a hated-but-cheap annoyance.

items.label: Re-typing insurer names into two systems: universally hated, 90 seconds, never causes a logged error
The slow insurer's 3-day callback queue: rarely mentioned unprompted, large cumulative delay per this module's earlier ranking
Referral-note-to-spreadsheet handoff: affects all referrals, averages 1.5 days delay, ranked highest-impact in the previous lesson
The office printer jamming roughly once a week, universally complained about, costs about 5 minutes to clear each time
The 18% first-pass rejection rate requiring resubmission: rarely framed as a top complaint, substantial cost per occurrence per the measuring module's cost-attribution work

explanation.vendor-retype: Not high-priority. High hate, low measured cost — exactly this lesson's pattern. Worth a cheap fix eventually, not worth leading a recommendation with.
explanation.callback-queue: Genuine high-priority candidate — established directly by this phase's own ranking work, despite being rarely complained about, because the actual cumulative delay is large.
explanation.referral-handoff: Genuine high-priority candidate — the highest-ranked by frequency × pain in the previous lesson's worked example, precisely because it's frequent and moderately costly on every single occurrence, not because anyone complains about it loudly.
explanation.printer-jam: Not high-priority. Same pattern as the vendor-retype and the fax machine from lesson one — universally annoying, genuinely cheap per occurrence. A different, smaller version of the same trap.
explanation.resubmission-cycle: Genuine high-priority candidate — this is the error-rate and rework finding from the measuring module, with real, traced cost (staff redo time, patient delay, occasional cancelled appointments) even though it isn't the thing people complain about first.

contentSections.synthesis: Two genuinely low-cost annoyances and three genuine high-impact candidates. Notice that none of the three high-impact candidates were the loudest complaint — they were found through mapping, baseline data, and cost-attribution work, not through asking what people hate most. That's not a coincidence; it's the whole reason this phase built those skills before this module.

contentSections.title: Writing the honest version of a low-cost finding

contentSections.code:
Recommendation memo, draft 1:

"Priority 1: Automate the vendor-name re-entry between scheduling and billing systems. This was the single most frequently mentioned pain point across every interview conducted, and addressing it will significantly improve the referral process."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this recommendation, given the baseline data from this lesson?

options.label: It should be Priority 2, not Priority 1

It conflates 'most frequently mentioned' with 'highest impact,' and claims it will 'significantly improve the referral process' when the baseline shows this step causes essentially no measured delay or error cost
The memo should include more direct quotes from staff

feedback.conflates-complaint-with-impact: Correct. The memo uses complaint frequency as if it were evidence of process impact, and then makes a claim — 'significantly improve the referral process' — that the baseline data doesn't support at all, since this step measurably costs almost nothing. Fixing it will genuinely improve morale and daily experience; it won't move the delay numbers that actually define the referral process's performance.
feedback.wrong-rank-number: The numbering isn't really the issue — even relabeled as a lower priority, the memo's actual claim (that fixing this will 'significantly improve the referral process') would still be unsupported by the data. The problem is the claim, not where it sits in the list.
feedback.needs-quotes: More quotes would make the complaint frequency even more vivid without fixing the underlying issue — the memo needs a different kind of evidence (baseline impact data) to support its claim, not more of the same kind it's already over-relying on.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This memo makes the exact mistake this lesson and lesson one both warn about: treating what's loudly complained about as a stand-in for what's actually costly. A defensible version would either drop the 'significantly improve the referral process' claim entirely, or reframe the recommendation honestly: 'This is worth fixing for staff experience — it's the most universally disliked step in the process — but the baseline data shows it isn't a meaningful driver of delay or error cost. Recommend addressing it as a low-cost morale win, not as part of the core efficiency fix.'

contentSections.body: Hated and expensive are two different measurements, and they don't always point at the same step. Say both, honestly, in a recommendation — 'worth fixing for morale, not a driver of the real cost' is a complete and useful finding, not a hedge.

title: Telling a client their stated problem isn't the problem
description: Larkspur's owner has insisted from the first call that he needs 'an AI that fills in insurance forms automatically.' The mapping, interviewing, and baseline work all point somewhere else entirely.

learningObjectives.text: Reframe a client's stated problem using evidence, without alienating them

contentSections.title: What he asked for, and what the evidence shows

contentSections.body: Since the very first call, back in this phase's first module, Larkspur's owner has said the same thing: "We need an AI that reads insurance PDFs and auto-fills the forms." You've now mapped the process, interviewed the staff, and baselined the numbers. Form-filling accounts for roughly two minutes per submission. The actual delay lives in the callback queue and the handoff gap — neither of which any form-filling tool touches.

This is the moment this whole phase has been building toward, and it's genuinely uncomfortable: telling a client, with evidence, that the thing they've been confidently asking for since day one wouldn't fix what they actually want fixed. Handled badly, this reads as a consultant contradicting the client to show off. Handled well, it's the single most valuable thing a diagnosis produces — the recommendation nobody could have arrived at just by asking what people think the problem is.

The difference is entirely in how the evidence gets presented. Leading with 'you're wrong about your own business' invites defensiveness regardless of how true it is. Leading with the traced timeline, the baseline numbers, and the specific finding — in that order, letting the evidence make the case before the conclusion is stated — gives the client room to arrive at the same conclusion themselves, which they're far more likely to actually accept and act on.

contentSections.title: Delivering the reframe
contentSections.opening: You're presenting final findings to Larkspur's owner. He opens the meeting by asking, "So — which AI form-filling tool do you recommend?" You have the full traced timeline, the baseline, and the ranked candidate list from this phase's work, none of which point at form-filling as the priority.

opens.situation: He's expecting a vendor name. You have a different answer.
opens.question: How do you respond to his opening question?

choices.label: "Form-filling isn't actually your problem — the real issue is a callback queue with one insurer."
choices.consequence: Technically the correct conclusion, delivered before any evidence. He hears a consultant contradicting the exact thing he's said for two months, with nothing yet to back it up, and spends the next several minutes defending the original request rather than hearing the finding.

choices.label: Change the subject to the ranked candidate list without directly addressing his question
choices.consequence: He notices the dodge immediately and repeats the question, now slightly more insistent. You've spent goodwill avoiding a direct answer instead of using it to build toward one.

choices.label: "Let me walk you through what we actually found, and I think the form-filling question will answer itself by the end." Then present the traced timeline, then the baseline numbers, then the ranked candidates — form-filling's true cost included, last.
choices.consequence: By the time you reach the form-filling line item — two minutes per submission, no measured error contribution — he's already seen the three-day callback queue and the referral handoff numbers with his own eyes. He asks the reframing question himself: "So form-filling wasn't really the issue, was it?"

his-question.situation: He's asked the question you were going to have to tell him. This is a different, easier conversation than the one where you tell him first.
his-question.question: How do you close this?

choices.label: Confirm plainly: "No — and I know that's not what you expected two months ago. The data's pretty clear on where the actual time goes."
choices.consequence: He nods, visibly a little deflated about the AI tool he'd been picturing, and then asks the useful next question: "okay, so what do we actually do about the insurer queue." The conversation moves forward instead of staying stuck defending the original request.

defensive-start.summary: The correct conclusion, delivered with no evidence in front of it, reads as an attack on two months of the client's own stated understanding. Recovering the meeting from there takes real effort, and some of the credibility of the finding itself gets lost along with it.
defensive-start.lesson: Being right about the reframe isn't enough — the evidence has to arrive before the conclusion, or the conclusion just sounds like an opinion contradicting the client's own.

dodged.summary: Avoiding the direct question doesn't actually avoid the eventual reframe — it just delays it and burns some trust in the meantime, since the client notices being redirected away from something he clearly wanted an answer to.
dodged.lesson: A hard question doesn't go away by not answering it directly — better to build toward the answer openly than to be caught dodging it.

landed.summary: By presenting the evidence in the order it was actually gathered — trace, baseline, ranking — the owner reaches the reframing conclusion himself before you have to state it, which makes it far easier for him to actually accept and act on. The conversation moves to solutions instead of staying stuck defending the original ask.
landed.lesson: Letting the evidence arrive before the conclusion, in the order it was actually built, lets the client discover the reframe rather than be told it — and a discovered conclusion survives a lot better than an announced one.

contentSections.body: The evidence has to arrive before the conclusion. A reframe the client reaches themselves, from the trace and the baseline they've now seen, survives contact with their own expectations far better than the same reframe announced up front.

title: When the honest answer is "don't automate anything"
description: After full analysis, one Larkspur location's volume is too low and its process too variable to justify any automation spend right now — and saying so, in writing, is still billable, credibility-building work.

learningObjectives.text: Identify genuine signals that automation isn't currently worth pursuing
Write a defensible no-build recommendation

contentSections.title: The recommendation nobody wants to give

contentSections.body: Larkspur's smallest location — two dentists, a fraction of the referral volume of the others — asks you to run the same analysis and recommend automation for its referral process too. After mapping, interviewing, and baselining, the honest finding is: 18 referrals a week, wildly variable insurer mix location to location, and the current manual process, while imperfect, costs Renata's counterpart there about 40 minutes a week in actual rework. Any automation investment here would take longer to pay for itself than it's reasonable to promise, and the process is too low-volume and variable to build something reliable around.

This is uncomfortable to say to a client who's paying for a diagnosis, partly because it can feel like failing to deliver, and partly because it's tempting to find *something* to recommend to justify the engagement. Resist both instincts. "Don't automate this right now" is a real, evidence-backed finding — arrived at through the same mapping, interviewing, and baseline work as every other recommendation in this phase — and it's often the finding that does the most for a consultant's actual long-term credibility, because it's the one a vendor with something to sell would never give.

The signals worth naming explicitly, distinguished from excuses to avoid doing harder work: genuinely low, stable volume where the cost of building and maintaining automation exceeds any plausible savings; genuinely high variability in the process itself (different insurers, different documentation needs, few repeating patterns) that would make a rule-based or model-based system unreliable; and a current manual cost that, honestly measured, is already low. None of these are about the engagement being hard — they're about the actual numbers not supporting a build.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding whether the 'don't automate' recommendation for Larkspur's smallest location is genuinely warranted, or whether it's actually an excuse to avoid harder analytical work.
contentSections.question: Select every signal that's a genuine reason not to recommend automation here, as opposed to an excuse.

items.label: 18 referrals/week, and it's been stable at that level for over a year — genuinely low relative to what would justify build-and-maintenance cost
Insurer mix and documentation requirements vary case to case with few repeating patterns, making a rule-based system unreliable
Honestly measured, the current manual rework cost is about 40 minutes a week — small relative to any plausible build cost
The engagement has taken longer than expected and you'd rather not do the deeper analysis this location would need
The client probably wouldn't approve a build budget for this location anyway
You haven't actually finished measuring this location's baseline yet

explanation.low-stable-volume: Genuine reason. Low, stable volume is exactly the kind of measured signal that supports a no-build recommendation — the economics genuinely don't favor automation at this scale.
explanation.high-variability: Genuine reason. High case-to-case variability with few repeating patterns is a real predictor that any built system — rule-based or model-based — would be unreliable, echoing the process-inconsistency failure mode from the very first module of this phase.
explanation.low-current-cost: Genuine reason. A small, honestly-measured current cost means there's little room for automation to save enough to justify its own cost, which is a legitimate economic argument, not an excuse.
explanation.consultant-tired: Not a genuine reason — this is about the consultant's own effort, not the client's actual situation, and using it to justify a recommendation the client is paying for is a conflict of interest dressed as an analytical finding.
explanation.client-unlikely-to-approve: Not a genuine reason for the recommendation itself — whether the client will approve a budget is a separate question from whether automation is actually warranted. Anticipating their answer and skipping the analysis accordingly undermines the honesty of the diagnosis.
explanation.no-clean-baseline-yet: Not a genuine reason to conclude 'don't automate' — an incomplete baseline is a reason to finish the baseline, not a finding in itself. Recommending against automation before the actual measurement is done isn't evidence-based, it's a guess with the same shape as a premature tool recommendation from the first module of this phase.

contentSections.synthesis: Three genuine, evidence-backed reasons and three that would make the recommendation an excuse rather than a finding. The dividing line is whether the reason comes from the client's actual measured situation, or from something about the consultant's own convenience or assumptions about what the client wants to hear.

contentSections.title: Writing it so it reads as a finding, not a failure

contentSections.body: A well-written no-build recommendation does three things: states the specific measured signals (not a vague "it's not worth it"), names what would change the answer (a volume threshold, a process-standardization change, a different insurer mix), and reminds the client — genuinely, not as a sales tactic — that this diagnosis was worth having precisely because it prevented a build that wouldn't have paid for itself. That last point isn't spin. A client who spends money finding out something isn't worth building has spent it better than a client who builds first and finds out the same thing eighteen months later.

"Don't automate this" is a real finding when the volume, variability, and current cost genuinely don't support a build — not an excuse for skipping harder work, and often the single most credibility-building thing a consultant can put in a report.

title: Practice — Rank the Automation Candidates in Seven Mapped Processes
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: rank, evaluate, or reframe automation candidates using this module's frequency-times-pain and honesty standards.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the bottleneck-identification, ranking, and honest-recommendation skills from this module to new scenarios

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills. Untimed, and the set doesn't expire.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Produce a Ranked Opportunity List for a Mapped Process
description: Apply this module's ranking, honesty, and reframing skills to a real, mapped and baselined process, producing a defensible ranked list — including at least one candidate you deliberately rejected and why.

learningObjectives.text: Rank real automation candidates by frequency and pain, with a separate feasibility pass
Justify at least one rejected candidate using genuine measured signals, not convenience

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Use the same real process from this phase's earlier labs if you have it — you should already have a map, an interview record, and a baseline. If not, use whatever real process you have the most information about. This lab is the capstone of the phase: turning everything gathered into a ranked, honest, defensible set of recommendations.

contentSections.title: Produce a ranked opportunity list
contentSections.brief: Using your mapped process and whatever baseline and interview data you've gathered, identify several real candidates for improvement or automation, rank them honestly by frequency times pain, and produce a written list — including at least one candidate you explicitly reject, and why.
contentSections.deliverable: A ranked list with the reasoning, including at least one candidate you rejected and why.

stages.title: List every real candidate, not just the loudest complaint
stages.instructions: From your mapping and interview work, list at least four distinct friction points or improvement candidates — deliberately include both loudly-complained-about ones and quieter, baseline-identified ones.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least four named candidates, not all drawn from the same source (complaints only, or data only).

stages.title: Score each by frequency times pain
stages.instructions: For each candidate, estimate or state its frequency and its per-occurrence cost, using real or plausible baseline data. Convert to a comparable unit where you can, and note explicitly where a comparison is apples-to-oranges rather than forcing false precision.
stages.checkpoint: Every candidate has a stated frequency, a stated per-occurrence cost, and an honest note on comparability.

stages.title: Run a separate feasibility pass
stages.instructions: For your top-ranked candidates by impact, separately assess feasibility — how hard would this actually be to address, given real constraints (external dependencies, technical complexity, organizational appetite). Keep this visibly separate from the impact score.
stages.checkpoint: Impact ranking and feasibility assessment are presented as two distinct passes, not blended into one score.

stages.title: Identify and justify at least one rejected candidate
stages.instructions: Pick at least one candidate — ideally one that's loudly complained about — and write an honest explanation of why it's not a priority, using genuine measured signals (low cost, low frequency, or a 'don't automate' case per lesson five), not convenience.
stages.checkpoint: The rejected candidate's justification cites specific measured signals, not vague dismissal.

stages.title: Write the ranked list and self-check
stages.instructions: Assemble the final ranked list with reasoning for each entry, including the rejected one. Then self-check: would each ranking survive being challenged with 'why isn't the loudest complaint at the top?'
stages.checkpoint: Every ranked item, including the rejection, has a stated reason grounded in frequency, pain, or feasibility — not in who complained loudest or what's easiest.

rubric.criterion: Candidates come from both complaints and baseline data
rubric.meets: The list includes at least one candidate identified primarily through baseline/mapping data rather than a loud complaint.

rubric.criterion: Ranked by frequency times pain, not by ease or complaint volume
rubric.meets: Each candidate's rank is justified by a stated frequency and per-occurrence cost, not by how often it was mentioned.

rubric.criterion: Feasibility is a separate, visible pass
rubric.meets: Impact ranking and feasibility assessment are presented distinctly, not merged into one score.

rubric.criterion: At least one candidate is explicitly rejected with real justification
rubric.meets: A rejected candidate is named with specific measured signals for why it isn't prioritized, not a vague dismissal.

rubric.criterion: Comparisons are honest about apples-to-oranges cases
rubric.meets: Where candidates aren't directly comparable on one axis, this is stated plainly rather than forced into false precision.

rubric.criterion: Would survive a 'why isn't the loudest complaint first' challenge
rubric.meets: Every ranking decision traces back to a stated, data-grounded reason.

contentSections.body: A ranked list that names what it rejected, and why, is more credible than one that only names what it recommends — it shows the ranking came from evidence, not from whichever answer was easiest to give.

title: Checkpoint — Finding Where It Actually Hurts
description: Ten questions: four from this module, two from the previous one, two each from two modules further back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Finding Where It Actually Hurts

questions.from: This module — Finding Where It Actually Hurts
questions.prompt: Why did Larkspur's staff complain unanimously about the fax machine while nobody mentioned the much costlier callback queue?

options.label: The fax machine is genuinely the bigger cost and the data must be wrong

An active, interruptive friction point (a jam) gets noticed and complained about every time; a passive wait (a queue) doesn't interrupt anyone, so it fades into the background regardless of its actual cost
Staff didn't know the callback queue existed

questions.explanation: Complaint volume tracks active annoyance, not measured cost — which is exactly why baseline data, not the complaint list, has to identify the actual bottleneck.

questions.from: This module — Finding Where It Actually Hurts
questions.prompt: In the frequency-times-pain ranking method, why is feasibility kept as a separate second pass rather than folded into the initial score?

options.label: Feasibility doesn't matter at all
Blending feasibility into the first score biases the ranking toward whatever's easiest, rather than whatever's actually most worth doing
Feasibility should always outweigh impact

questions.explanation: Keeping the two passes distinct is what keeps the initial ranking honest about impact, before real-world constraints get applied afterward.

questions.from: This module — Finding Where It Actually Hurts
questions.prompt: Why was the universally-hated vendor-name re-entry step NOT a genuine high-impact automation priority at Larkspur?

options.label: It was too difficult to fix
It was hated but measurably cheap — about 90 seconds and no logged errors — so fixing it wouldn't move the actual cost or delay numbers
Nobody actually complained about it

questions.explanation: 'Universally hated' and 'genuinely costly' are two different measurements — this step scored high on the first and low on the second, which is exactly the trap this module names.

questions.from: This module — Finding Where It Actually Hurts
questions.prompt: In the case-sim about reframing the form-filling request, why did presenting the evidence before the conclusion work better than stating the conclusion first?

options.label: It took less time overall

Leading with the conclusion invites defensiveness before any evidence backs it up; letting the client see the trace and baseline first lets them reach the same conclusion themselves, which they're far more likely to accept
The client wouldn't have understood the conclusion otherwise

questions.explanation: A reframe the client discovers from evidence they've seen survives contact with their own prior expectations far better than the same reframe simply announced up front.

questions.from: This module — Finding Where It Actually Hurts
questions.prompt: What are genuine signals that support a 'don't automate this' recommendation, per this module?

options.label: The consultant would rather not do more analysis
Genuinely low, stable volume; genuinely high process variability; and a low current measured cost
The client probably wouldn't approve the budget anyway

questions.explanation: These three come from the client's actual measured situation. Consultant convenience and guessing at client approval are both excuses, not evidence-based findings.

questions.from: This module — Finding Where It Actually Hurts
questions.prompt: Why does a well-written no-build recommendation still count as valuable, billable work?

options.label: It isn't valuable — it should be avoided if possible
It prevents the client from spending far more building something that wouldn't have paid for itself, and it's a finding a vendor with something to sell would never give
It's valuable only if it comes with a smaller alternative recommendation attached

questions.explanation: A client who learns something isn't worth automating before building it has spent their diagnosis money better than one who finds out the same thing eighteen months into a failed build.

questions.from: Previous module — Measuring Before You Change Anything
questions.prompt: Why is 'saved 10 hours a week' unverifiable without a pre-intervention baseline?

options.label: It's inherently a subtraction, before-time minus after-time, and without a recorded before-number there's nothing to subtract from
10 hours is always unrealistic
The claim is always dishonest

questions.explanation: This module's ranking work depends entirely on the baseline numbers from the previous module — without them, frequency and pain can't be measured, only guessed at.

questions.from: Previous module — Measuring Before You Change Anything
questions.prompt: What four things does a defensible baseline number need stated alongside it?

options.label: Method, period/sample size, confidence level, and whether it's measured or estimated
A chart, an industry comparison, a forecast, and a recommendation
More decimal places to look precise

questions.explanation: This same defensibility standard applies directly to the frequency and pain figures used in this module's ranking work.

questions.from: Earlier in this phase — Getting the Truth Out of People
questions.prompt: Why is 'walk me through what happened to this exact request' a better opening question than 'how does the process work'?

options.label: It anchors the answer to a specific memory instead of inviting a polished, idealized summary
It's a shorter question
It's more polite

questions.explanation: The story-shaped interview questions from earlier in this phase are part of what surfaced the real friction points this module had to rank honestly.

questions.from: Earlier in this phase — Mapping Work As It Is
questions.prompt: What's the difference between the documented process and the shadow process?

options.label: The documented process describes intent; the shadow process is what actually keeps the work running
The shadow process is always noncompliance
They're always identical

questions.explanation: Renata's spreadsheet, mapped early in this phase, turned out to be exactly the kind of real record that led to identifying the genuine bottleneck later in this module.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.
